days.title: Secure and Compliant Data Design: IAM, Encryption, Residency and Environments

concepts.heading: Identities and Least Privilege for Pipelines
concepts.body: Every pipeline runs as an identity, and the safe default is not the one Google Cloud hands you. A Dataflow job has a submitting user and a worker service account, the account the worker VMs use to read sources and write sinks. By default that is the Compute Engine default service account, which is shared and often over-privileged. Google recommends a user-managed worker service account per pipeline, holding roles/dataflow.worker plus data roles granted on the narrowest resource: the one bucket it reads and the one dataset it writes, not the project. In BigQuery, who may read data and where a query runs are separate decisions. A marketing group that must query the central team's dataset but pay for its own queries gets Data Viewer on that dataset in the data project and Job User in the marketing project: no copies, no write access, clean chargeback. Basic roles and organization-wide admin roles are the opposite of this pattern.

concepts.heading: Projects, Zones and Environments
concepts.body: The project is the unit for IAM scope, quotas, billing, audit logs and organization policy inheritance, so it is the main governance boundary for data. A retailer with raw partner files, curated finance data and a data science group experimenting with copies should not use one project and one dataset, because project-level Data Editor would let an experiment change finance tables. The usual layout separates zones (raw, curated, consumption, sandbox) and environments (dev, test, prod) into different projects grouped in folders, with roles granted to groups at the dataset or bucket level. Dev versus prod applies to pipeline code too. Dataform compiles SQL workflows through release configurations and schedules them through workflow configurations, and a workflow configuration can run as a dedicated service account. Developers keep dev workspaces, while scheduled production runs use an identity no one signs in with; acting as that account needs iam.serviceAccounts.actAs, which is granted sparingly.

concepts.heading: Encryption Keys and Data Residency
concepts.body: Residency has two halves: where data is stored and where it is processed. Placement is fixed early. A BigQuery dataset has a location chosen at creation, and a load job needs its Cloud Storage bucket in the same location, so an EU dataset fed from a us-central1 bucket fails until the files move to an EU location; moving the dataset to the US would break the rule. The resource locations organization policy constraint is the guardrail, and Google recommends an in: value group such as in:eu-locations so new EU locations are covered. Set at an organization or folder, it is inherited by projects teams create later. Dataflow handles job metadata and controls workers in the region you pick, so choose an EU region. For customer-managed encryption keys, a Cloud KMS key ring has a fixed location and Google documents that it should match the dataset location: an EU multi-region dataset gets a key ring in europe. The key lives in one place and cannot be moved.

concepts.heading: Protecting Values, Boundaries and Evidence
concepts.body: Sensitive Data Protection (formerly Cloud DLP) de-identifies values with tokenization. Deterministic encryption (AES-SIV) and format-preserving encryption (FPE-FFX) are reversible with the Cloud KMS key and give equal inputs equal tokens, so analysts can still join customer and order tables while only the fraud service holds decrypt rights on the key. FPE keeps a 16-digit card number 16 digits long, which suits a nightly test refresh whose application validates the format. Hashing is one-way. For column and row control inside BigQuery, use column-level policy tags for national ID values and row-level access policies for regions. IAM cannot say that data must not leave a boundary; VPC Service Controls draws a perimeter that blocks copying query results to a project outside it. For evidence, BigQuery writes Data Access audit logs by default, and a log sink exports them to a separate audit project or bucket for multi-year retention.

examPoints: A question that gives a Dataflow job the default Compute Engine service account and asks for least privilege points to a user-managed worker service account with roles on the single bucket and dataset.
A question about an EU dataset, a key ring location or a bucket in another region points to matching locations everywhere, with a resource locations policy as the guardrail.
A question where analysts may read data but must not copy it out, or must join on IDs they cannot see, points to VPC Service Controls or Sensitive Data Protection tokenization with a KMS key.

quiz.q: A health-data company must keep a BigQuery dataset in the EU multi-region and encrypt every table with a customer-managed key. Where should the Cloud KMS key ring be created?
choices: In the europe multi-region, so that the key ring location matches the dataset location
In the us multi-region, because the key ring location is independent of the dataset location
In the global location, so one key ring can protect datasets that sit in any region
In any single EU region, because a region key ring can protect a multi-region dataset
quiz.explain: BigQuery guidance is to create the key ring in a location that matches the dataset, and an EU multi-region dataset matches the europe location. A global key ring is tempting for flexibility, but it does not match the dataset and weakens a residency argument.

quiz.q: A payments company copies customer and order tables into BigQuery. Analysts must join them on customer ID without ever seeing the real IDs, while a small fraud service must recover the real ID for flagged cases. Which design fits?
choices: Replace each ID with a fixed text value so that analysts can never reach the original values
Hash each ID one-way with a salt and keep the salt in a table that only analysts can read
Tokenize each ID with deterministic encryption and give only the fraud service key access
Encrypt each ID with a different random key per row and store those keys beside the data
quiz.explain: Deterministic encryption gives equal IDs equal tokens, so joins still work, and IAM on the Cloud KMS key controls who can re-identify. A fixed replacement is tempting for secrecy, but it collapses every join into one value.

days.recap: Run pipelines as least-privilege service accounts, separate zones and environments by project, match locations for datasets, buckets, jobs and keys under a resource locations policy, and use tokenization, perimeters and audit sinks to protect and prove access.

days.title: Reliable Pipelines: Validation, Monitoring, Disaster Recovery and Consistency

concepts.heading: Validating and Cleaning Data in the Pipeline
concepts.body: Fidelity means bad data is caught, kept for review and never silently loaded. In Dataform, an assertion is a query that returns violating rows, and the run fails if any come back. Built-in conditions in a table's config cover nonNull, uniqueKey and rowConditions, so missing customer IDs and duplicate order IDs are tested on every run. Unit tests are different: they mock an action's inputs and compare the SQL output, so null handling and regular-expression edge cases are checked before release. Use unit tests for logic and assertions for the data that arrives. In Dataflow, an uncaught exception in a DoFn retries the bundle four times in batch and then fails, but retries indefinitely in streaming and can stall the job, so the code catches the error and sends the record to a dead-letter destination such as a BigQuery table or Pub/Sub topic. Cloud Data Fusion gives a no-code route: an error collector gathers rejected records into a separate sink for review.

concepts.heading: Observing and Hardening Orchestration
concepts.body: Pipelines fail at night, so the design decides who finds out. Cloud Composer (Managed Service for Apache Airflow in current product pages) sends scheduler, worker, database and DAG-run metrics to Cloud Monitoring and logs to Cloud Logging, and alerting policies on them notify people as failures happen instead of when business users complain. Resilience has two layers. For infrastructure, a highly resilient environment runs the metadata database as a high-availability instance and spreads Airflow components across zones, so losing a zone does not stop scheduling. For workflow design, tasks use retries and retry_delay in default_args so transient API errors heal themselves. Retries are safe only when tasks are idempotent. A nightly append that reruns after a timeout and doubles the rows is a design flaw, not an orchestrator flaw. The fix is to load into a staging table and apply a MERGE on the business key, or overwrite the day's partition, so any rerun converges to the same result.

concepts.heading: Fault Tolerance and Disaster Recovery for Stored Data
concepts.body: Match the recovery tool to the failure. A BigQuery multi-region does not keep data available if a physical region is destroyed, so it is not regional redundancy. For a requirement to keep reporting within minutes after a regional outage, use managed disaster recovery: cross-region dataset replication plus an Enterprise Plus edition reservation, which includes standby compute in the paired region. A soft failover waits for pending changes to replicate and needs both regions, so it fits planned tests. A hard failover promotes the secondary immediately and can lose unreplicated data. Logical damage and retention are different problems. Time travel covers a window of 2 to 7 days, and fail-safe adds seven more for emergency recovery. Table snapshots keep month-end versions for a year while storing only the changed bytes. For raw files in a Cloud Storage dual-region bucket, default replication targets 99.9% of new objects within an hour; turbo replication targets a 15-minute RPO for all objects.

concepts.heading: Consistency, Transactions and Availability Trade-offs
concepts.body: Distributed stores trade strictness for reach, and the stem's wording tells you which side matters. A global ledger where two stores update the same item at once, with no double counting or reordering, calls for Spanner, whose external consistency makes transactions behave as if run one at a time in real-time order, even across regions. Bigtable replication between clusters is eventually consistent. A rider app that reads back a just-written pickup point and sometimes sees the old value is fixed with single-cluster routing in the app profile, which gives read-your-writes consistency while the other cluster stays a replica; multi-cluster routing favors availability instead. Inside BigQuery, a staging-to-history move with separate statements can leave rows in both tables after a failure. A multi-statement transaction commits or rolls back all changes together, with snapshot isolation. Reordering the statements only changes whether a crash causes duplicates or loss.

examPoints: A question that wants bad rows caught on every run and kept for review points to Dataform assertions, a Dataflow dead-letter output or a Data Fusion error collector, depending on the tool in the stem.

A question that asks for reporting within minutes after a regional loss, with a multi-region dataset already in place, points to BigQuery managed disaster recovery, since a multi-region is not regional redundancy.
A question about a retry that duplicates rows points to idempotent loads with MERGE, and one about two tables changing together points to a multi-statement transaction.

quiz.q: A streaming Dataflow pipeline parses JSON events in a DoFn and writes to BigQuery. After one malformed record arrives, the job stops making progress and the same exception repeats. What is the best fix?
choices: Catch the parsing error in the DoFn and emit the bad record to a dead-letter destination for later inspection
Switch the job to batch mode, because batch stops retrying a failing bundle after a fixed number of attempts
Increase the worker count, because more workers will spread the failing bundle across additional machines
Raise the Pub/Sub acknowledgement deadline so that the failing message is redelivered less often to workers
quiz.explain: In streaming mode a failing bundle is retried indefinitely, so the code must handle the exception and route the record aside. Switching to batch is tempting, but batch simply fails the whole pipeline after its retries.

quiz.q: A ride-hailing app keeps trip state in Bigtable replicated across two regions. Right after a rider changes a pickup point, the app reads it back and sometimes sees the old value. Availability during a regional outage matters too. What should the team change?
choices: Move the table to BigQuery, because it offers stronger consistency for single-row lookups than Bigtable
Use multi-cluster routing, because requests then reach the nearest cluster, which always holds the newest value
Add a third cluster, because a larger replica set makes replication between clusters complete sooner
Use single-cluster routing in the app profile and change the profile to the other cluster on failover
quiz.explain: Single-cluster routing gives read-your-writes consistency, and failover becomes a deliberate profile change. Multi-cluster routing is tempting for availability, but replication between clusters is eventually consistent.

days.recap: Test data with assertions, dead letters and error collectors, alert on orchestrators and make tasks idempotent, pick the recovery tool for the failure (managed DR, snapshots, turbo replication), and choose consistency models by what the application cannot tolerate.

days.title: Flexible and Portable Designs: Requirements, Open Formats, Multi-cloud and Staging

concepts.heading: From Requirements to Architecture
concepts.body: A good design starts by turning each quantified requirement into a property the architecture must have. Seconds of latency points to streaming ingestion and processing rather than periodic batch. Spiky, unpredictable volume points to a buffer that absorbs bursts, Pub/Sub, and workers that autoscale, Dataflow. A small team with no cluster management points to serverless parts. Analytical dashboards point to BigQuery as the sink. A ticketing company that sees quiet days and sudden on-sale spikes, and wants sales on a dashboard within seconds, lands on exactly this pattern. When existing code is the main requirement, the answer changes: about 200 nightly Spark jobs with custom JARs, to be moved within a quarter with minimal change, fit Dataproc, which runs open source Spark and Hadoop. Dataflow, BigQuery SQL and Data Fusion are later modernization targets because each needs the logic rewritten into a different model. The wording of the constraint chooses the service.

concepts.heading: Open Formats and Open Programming Models
concepts.body: Lock-in comes from proprietary formats and proprietary programming models, so portability is built from open ones. Dataflow is a managed runner for Apache Beam pipelines, and Beam separates the pipeline definition from the runner, so the same logic can run on Dataflow, Apache Flink or Apache Spark. Keep transformation logic in Beam transforms and use Beam I/O connectors; the thin service-specific glue is easy to replace. For data, self-describing typed formats such as Avro, Parquet and ORC are read natively by BigQuery, Dataflow and Spark, whereas CSV carries no types and breaks when columns change. Avro suits write-heavy landing zones because a new field with a default value can be added safely. When both a BigQuery team (SQL DML) and a Spark team need the same tables, Apache Iceberg managed tables in BigQuery keep one copy in buckets you own, with Iceberg metadata that Spark and other engines can read. Writes go through BigQuery.

concepts.heading: Multi-cloud and Storage Decoupling
concepts.body: Sometimes data cannot or should not be copied. A retailer whose clickstream must stay in an AWS region can still join it with BigQuery sales tables. BigQuery Omni runs BigQuery compute in AWS or Azure regions, and BigLake tables over Amazon S3 or Azure Blob Storage are queried in place through a connection. In an Omni join the filtering happens in the AWS region and only the subquery result crosses over, so raw objects never move and no copy job is needed. Omni needs no cluster to run and no copy job to schedule. The same decoupling helps migrations from Hadoop. HDFS ties data to machines, so you keep the machines to keep the data. On Google Cloud, store the data in Cloud Storage, read it from Spark through the Cloud Storage connector, and create short-lived Dataproc clusters per job. Object storage has higher per-operation latency, which is acceptable for batch jobs that run monthly.

concepts.heading: Staging Zones, Cataloging and Profiling
concepts.body: A layered layout keeps designs flexible. A raw (landing) zone holds source files exactly as received on cheap object storage and is the system of record. A curated zone holds validated, standardized data, and serving tables feed consumers. A logistics company whose cleaning rules change several times a year can rebuild curated tables from raw without asking partners to resend files, and with versioned transformation code it can reproduce a table as it was a year ago. Cleaning that discards information at ingest makes both impossible. Metadata makes the layers usable. Knowledge Catalog (renamed from Dataplex Universal Catalog in April 2026; API, CLI and IAM names unchanged) catalogs the assets, and a data profile scan analyzes a BigQuery table to produce statistics about its columns. Scans can run on a schedule or on demand, and the results can be used to recommend data quality rules. Profile first, then decide what to validate.

examPoints: A question that asks for the same pipeline logic to run on Flink or Spark later points to Apache Beam on Dataflow, because the programming model is what is portable.

A question where data must stay in S3 or Blob Storage yet join BigQuery tables points to BigQuery Omni with BigLake tables, and a question about one copy shared by SQL and Spark points to Iceberg managed tables.
A question about changing business rules and re-deriving past tables points to a raw landing zone plus versioned transformations, and one about moving existing Spark jobs quickly points to Dataproc.

quiz.q: A bank wants to limit lock-in without giving up managed services for a new analytics platform. Which choice best supports portability of both its data and its processing logic?
choices: Write transformations as BigQuery stored procedures only, and keep the landing files as a vendor-specific binary export
Write pipelines with Apache Beam and land data in open columnar or row formats such as Parquet or Avro
Write transformations in the visual designer of one product, and store the landing files as compressed text archives
Write pipelines in service-specific templates and keep the data only in managed tables with no file exports
quiz.explain: Open programming models keep logic independent of the runner, and open formats can be read by many engines. Stored procedures are tempting for simplicity, but they tie logic to one product and a binary export needs its producer to read it.

quiz.q: A retailer's raw clickstream files sit in Amazon S3 and contractually must stay in that AWS region (only query results may leave). Analysts already use BigQuery and want to join the clickstream with BigQuery sales tables without copy jobs. What should they use?
choices: Storage Transfer Service to copy the objects into Cloud Storage nightly, then load them into BigQuery
A Dataflow batch job that reads the S3 objects and writes aggregates into a BigQuery table every hour
A BigQuery load job that points at the S3 bucket and copies the objects into native storage each night
BigQuery Omni with BigLake tables over the S3 data, joined to the sales tables in one query
quiz.explain: Omni runs BigQuery compute next to the data and moves only the subquery result, so the raw objects stay in the AWS region. Transfer tools are tempting for analytics, but every copy-based design moves the files out.

days.recap: Map each quantified requirement to an architectural property, choose open formats and Beam for portability, query data in place with Omni when it cannot move, decouple storage from compute, and keep a raw zone so curated data can be rebuilt.

days.title: Planning and Validating Migrations: Databases, Warehouses, Files and Replication

concepts.heading: Choosing the Service: Migrate, Replicate or Schedule a Load
concepts.body: Three services are easy to confuse, and the stem's verbs tell them apart. Database Migration Service (DMS) moves a database into Cloud SQL or AlloyDB and makes the destination the new primary. A continuous migration does an initial dump and load, keeps replicating changes with change data capture while the source stays live, and you promote the destination at cutover, so a 2 TB MySQL system that tolerates only minutes of downtime fits. A one-time migration is a point-in-time snapshot with no writes to the source while it runs, so a 40 GB PostgreSQL database with a weekend of accepted downtime needs nothing more. Datastream is serverless change data capture and replication: it reads logs from sources such as Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server with minimal load, backfills, then streams changes to BigQuery or Cloud Storage while the source stays the system of record. BigQuery Data Transfer Service runs scheduled, managed loads into BigQuery.

concepts.heading: Datastream, Transfer Service Gaps and Private Networking
concepts.body: Datastream writes to BigQuery in one of two modes. Merge mode keeps the destination mirroring the source's current state and applies updates and deletes, which relies on a primary key at the source. Append-only mode adds every change event as a new row, with a datastream_metadata column for ordering, so a compliance team that must reconstruct a row at any past moment wants append-only. Networking is part of the design. If an on-premises Oracle database is reachable only over Cloud VPN from a private network, a public connection profile cannot connect and exposing the listener to the internet breaks the security policy. Create a private connectivity configuration so Datastream reaches the source through VPC peering over the VPN or Interconnect. BigQuery Data Transfer Service loads from sources such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Cloud Storage, Teradata, Redshift, Snowflake and SaaS applications. If a daily run failed for three days, request a backfill run for the missed dates on the same configuration.

concepts.heading: Moving Files: Online Transfer or Transfer Appliance
concepts.body: For files, compare transfer time (size divided by usable bandwidth) with the deadline. Storage Transfer Service is built for large online moves: from on-premises file systems through self-hosted agents, from Amazon S3 or Azure Blob Storage with Google-managed workers, and from HDFS. It can be scheduled, copies only new or changed data, validates integrity and lets the network team control bandwidth. A manufacturer with 600 TB, a 10 Gbps Interconnect and a nightly sync requirement, or an advertising firm with 150 TB in S3, fits it with nothing to build. A custom Dataflow copier would reimplement listing, retries and checksums. When the numbers do not work, use Transfer Appliance. A remote lab with 800 TB and a shared 200 Mbps link would need more than a year online. You copy data to the encrypted appliance, ship it back, and Google uploads it to your bucket and wipes it. Data size and available bandwidth decide, not downstream design details.

concepts.heading: Migrating Warehouses and Proving the Result
concepts.body: A warehouse migration has code and data, and each needs proof. The BigQuery Migration Service covers the phases: assessment of the existing estate, SQL translation from supported dialects into GoogleSQL (batch, interactive and API translators), data transfer through BigQuery Data Transfer Service, and a data validation tool that checks that source and destination tables match after migration. A retailer moving a Teradata warehouse with thousands of dialect scripts needs both translation and validation; translating code without proving the data, or the reverse, is a common cause of failed cutovers. The wider planning pattern is the same for any migration: decide whether downtime is acceptable, choose online or offline movement from size and bandwidth, plan private connectivity for sources that cannot be exposed, and define how correctness is verified before users switch. For existing Spark or Hadoop code, a lift-and-shift to Dataproc comes first, modernization later.

examPoints: A question where the old database must be live until cutover, with only minutes of downtime, points to a continuous Database Migration Service migration, and a tolerated weekend outage points to a one-time migration.
A question that keeps an operational database in place yet needs changes in BigQuery within seconds points to Datastream, with append-only mode when the full change history must be kept.
A question that compares terabytes against a slow or shared link points to the transfer-time calculation: Storage Transfer Service when it fits, Transfer Appliance when it does not.

quiz.q: An insurer's Oracle database stays on premises as the system of record. Analysts need every change in BigQuery within seconds, without adding noticeable load to the source. Which service fits?
choices: Database Migration Service with a one-time migration, repeated each night to refresh the BigQuery tables
BigQuery Data Transfer Service scheduled hourly, loading full copies of the source tables into BigQuery
Datastream reading the database logs and streaming an initial backfill plus changes to BigQuery
Transfer Appliance shipped to the data center, then reloaded after each batch of changes at the source
quiz.explain: Datastream is serverless change data capture that reads logs with minimal source impact and keeps the source in place. Database Migration Service is tempting because it also uses replication, but it makes a Cloud SQL or AlloyDB database the new primary.

quiz.q: A genomics lab at a remote site has 800 TB of files and a shared 200 Mbps internet link. The data must reach Cloud Storage within two months. Which approach is the best fit?
choices: Run Storage Transfer Service with agents on site, because it validates integrity and can repeat on a schedule
Use Transfer Appliance, copy locally, ship it to Google and let Google upload the data to the bucket
Write a Dataflow pipeline that uploads the files in parallel to the bucket through the shared link
Buy a larger internet plan and compress every file first, then upload it directly to the bucket
quiz.explain: Even a fully dedicated 200 Mbps link would need over a year for 800 TB, so offline shipping removes the network from the critical path. Storage Transfer Service is tempting for its features, but it still depends on the same link.

days.recap: Pick DMS to move a database, Datastream to replicate changes, BigQuery Data Transfer Service to schedule loads, and Storage Transfer Service or Transfer Appliance by comparing size with bandwidth, with private connectivity and a validation step planned in.

days.title: Planning Pipelines: Sources, Sinks, Networking and Encryption

concepts.heading: Choose the Smallest Pipeline That Meets the Requirement
concepts.body: Planning a pipeline starts from the source, the sink and what must happen in between. If the data only has to move, the least machinery wins. Pub/Sub has three subscription families. Pull and push subscriptions hand messages to a subscriber you run, while export subscriptions make the Pub/Sub service itself write each message to BigQuery or Cloud Storage. A fleet of delivery vans publishing JSON telemetry that must reach a BigQuery table within seconds, with no filtering or enrichment, fits a BigQuery subscription: nothing to deploy, scale or monitor. Add a transform, a join or an aggregation and a subscriber is needed, which is where a streaming Dataflow job earns its place. Between pull and push, pull suits very high volume and private workers because the client controls the delivery rate, while push needs a public HTTPS endpoint and delivers one message per request, so it fits webhooks and Cloud Run. A Dataproc cluster for a pass-through load is the heaviest option and rarely the answer.

concepts.heading: Contracts and Change Data Capture at the Edges
concepts.body: Pipelines break at the boundaries, so plan the contract and the buffer. A Pub/Sub schema, in Apache Avro or Protocol Buffer format and attached to a topic, enforces the format of the message data: a message that does not conform is not published. When four product teams share one topic and subscribers keep failing on missing or misnamed fields, the schema stops bad data at the source for every consumer. For database sources, Datastream captures change data from databases such as PostgreSQL and can write the change events to Cloud Storage. Dataflow templates can then read those files and load BigQuery, Spanner or Cloud SQL. Landing changes in Cloud Storage first gives a durable, replayable record. Know the limits of the neighbours: Database Migration Service targets Cloud SQL and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, and BigQuery Data Transfer Service loads into BigQuery, so neither writes to Spanner.

concepts.heading: Networking: Keep Workers Private and Inside the Approved Network
concepts.body: Network choices are made at design time because they decide whether the job can start. Dataflow workers must reach Google Cloud APIs. When policy forbids external IP addresses, enable Private Google Access on the subnet (or use Private Service Connect for Google APIs) and launch the job with public IPs disabled for its workers; dependencies must then be staged, since workers cannot download packages from the internet. When a central network team owns a Shared VPC, a Dataflow job in a service project runs in a host-project subnet by naming the subnetwork with its full URL, and the launching user needs permission on that subnet. Omitting the network parameters selects the project's default network. Cloud Data Fusion runs its managed resources in a tenant project. A private instance is reached through VPC peering to your VPC, so pipelines can read an on-premises database over Cloud VPN or Interconnect without public endpoints.

concepts.heading: Identity and Encryption per Resource
concepts.body: Every Dataflow job involves two identities. The Dataflow service agent creates and manages resources, while the worker service account is what worker VMs, and therefore the I/O connectors, act as when they read the source and write the sink. By default the worker account is the Compute Engine default service account, which holds broad roles; the docs advise a user-managed service account with the Dataflow Worker role plus minimal data roles at the lowest level, such as editor on one dataset. The launching user needs permission to act as that account. A project Owner launching a job does not give the workers any access to a dataset in another project: grant that dataset to the worker account. Customer-managed encryption keys are also set per resource. Pub/Sub, Dataflow and BigQuery each integrate with Cloud KMS and encrypt their own resources, so a CMEK policy means a key configured on the topic, the job and the table, with key permissions for the service agents and workers.

examPoints: A question that describes plain messages going into a BigQuery table with no transformation and asks for the fewest components points to a BigQuery subscription on the topic, not Dataflow or Dataproc.
A question where Dataflow starts but fails to read or write a dataset despite the launching user being an owner points to the worker service account needing access, not the user.

A question about workers with no external IPs, or a central network team that controls subnets, points to Private Google Access with public IPs disabled, or a Shared VPC subnetwork named by its full URL.

quiz.q: Several teams publish events to one Pub/Sub topic, and downstream subscribers keep failing because some publishers omit required fields. The data lead wants invalid events stopped before any consumer sees them. What should the team do?
choices: Attach an Avro or Protocol Buffer schema to the topic so bad messages are rejected when published
Add a Dataflow job after the topic that drops invalid events and republishes the valid ones to a second topic
Give every subscriber its own validation code and a dead-letter topic for the events that fail validation
Create a BigQuery subscription with a dead-letter table so that invalid events are collected for later review
quiz.explain: A topic schema is a contract enforced when a message is published, so bad data never reaches any subscriber. The Dataflow filter and the per-subscriber checks also catch bad events, but only after the topic accepted them and with more code to run.

quiz.q: A company must replicate an operational PostgreSQL database into Spanner and wants the raw change events kept in Cloud Storage so they can be replayed. Which design fits?
choices: BigQuery Data Transfer Service scheduled transfers from PostgreSQL into Spanner on a regular nightly cadence
A BigQuery subscription on a Pub/Sub topic that receives the change events and writes them into Spanner
Database Migration Service continuous jobs with Spanner chosen as the destination database for the change events
Datastream writing change events to Cloud Storage, then a Dataflow template that loads the files into Spanner
quiz.explain: Datastream captures the changes, Cloud Storage keeps a durable replayable record, and a Dataflow template can load Spanner. Database Migration Service targets Cloud SQL and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, and the transfer service loads only BigQuery.

days.recap: Move data with the smallest pipeline: export subscription if nothing changes, Dataflow if it does. Plan contracts, private networking, the worker service account and per-resource CMEK at design time.

days.title: Streaming I: Pub/Sub Delivery and Dataflow Operations

concepts.heading: Pub/Sub Delivery Features: Dead Letters, Ordering and Exactly-Once
concepts.body: When a subscriber keeps failing on one malformed message, Pub/Sub retries it until the acknowledgment deadline logic gives up. A dead-letter topic fixes this: after a configured number of delivery attempts, between 5 and 100, Pub/Sub forwards the message to the dead-letter topic where another subscription can inspect it. The count is approximate, and it only works when Pub/Sub's service account has the publisher role on the dead-letter topic and the subscriber role on the subscription. Ordering keys deliver messages that share a key in publish order, but only within a region, and a redelivery triggers redelivery of later messages for that key. Exactly-once delivery is enabled per subscription, works within a region, and is supported only on pull subscriptions, including StreamingPull; push and export subscriptions do not support it. Subscribers still must acknowledge within the deadline and avoid repeating work when an acknowledgment fails.

concepts.heading: Replay, Ordering with Dataflow and Regional Failure
concepts.body: Once acknowledged, a message is no longer available to subscribers. Seek changes the acknowledgment state in bulk, either to a snapshot or to a timestamp. A snapshot is a point-in-time view of a subscription's acknowledgment state and lives at most seven days; taking one before a risky deployment is good practice. If a buggy release acknowledged thousands of messages without processing them and no snapshot exists, the recovery route is retention: configure message retention on the topic, or retain acknowledged messages on the subscription, then seek to a time before the deployment. For Dataflow, do not enable message ordering on the subscription: Dataflow groups elements by event timestamp in windows, and the Pub/Sub docs warn that ordering can reduce pipeline performance. For a regional outage, Dataflow lists options by tolerance for loss: wait, run duplicate pipelines in two regions for no loss at the highest cost, or keep two independent subscriptions on the topic, one per region, and start a replacement job on the backup subscription with some potential loss.

concepts.heading: Streaming Engine and Autoscaling
concepts.body: Streaming Engine moves pipeline execution out of the worker VMs into the Dataflow service backend. Workers use less CPU, memory and Persistent Disk, horizontal autoscaling is more responsive and granular, and service updates need no redeployment. It works best with small worker machine types and has a service charge. You cannot switch a running job to Streaming Engine: drain it, then launch it again with the option. Without Streaming Engine, Persistent Disks are allocated at launch, so a later update can raise the worker count only up to the original maximum. With it, state lives in the service and the range can change with an update. For delay-tolerant work such as audit events, a medium or high latency tier makes the autoscaler wait for more backlog before scaling up, saving cost. Autoscaling follows the workers, so a sink limit shows up as more workers with flat throughput: for Bigtable, parallelism comes from cluster nodes, so add nodes.

concepts.heading: Updating, Replacing and Draining a Streaming Job
concepts.body: New pipeline code needs a replacement job. Dataflow runs a compatibility check between the old and new jobs so intermediate state and buffered data can be transferred. If transforms were renamed, supply a transform name mapping linking the new names to the old ones. If the replacement uses a later Beam SDK version, set the update compatibility version to that of the original job. To test validity without launching, add the graph validate only service option and then launch again without it. Drain applies to streaming jobs: the job stops reading, marks sources with an event timestamp at infinity and finishes processing buffered data. Streaming Dataflow retries a failing element indefinitely, so a repeating exception in a parsing step can leave a drain stuck. You can update the draining job with code that fixes the error and the drain completes without data loss; cancelling also works but gives up the buffered data.

examPoints: A question about a poison message that blocks a pull subscriber and must be set aside after a few tries points to a dead-letter topic with a maximum delivery attempts value and the right IAM for the Pub/Sub service account.

A question about reprocessing already acknowledged messages with no snapshot points to topic or subscription retention plus a seek to a timestamp, and about a stuck drain points to updating the draining job with a fix.

A question where more Dataflow workers do not raise throughput and the sink is saturated points to scaling the sink, such as Bigtable nodes, while a delay-tolerant Streaming Engine job points to a higher latency tier.

quiz.q: A pull subscriber keeps failing on one malformed message, and the same message returns again and again. The team wants it set aside after a limited number of attempts so it can be inspected later. What should they configure?
choices: A dead-letter topic with a maximum delivery attempts value, plus roles for the Pub/Sub service account
Message ordering with an ordering key so that the failing message is skipped and later messages continue
Exactly-once delivery on the subscription so that the failing message is never delivered more than one time
A shorter acknowledgment deadline on the subscription so that the broken message expires sooner and is dropped
quiz.explain: A dead-letter topic forwards a message after a set number of delivery attempts, and Pub/Sub counts attempts correctly only when its service account holds the publisher and subscriber roles. A shorter deadline just causes faster redelivery, and ordering makes a failing message block later ones for the same key.

quiz.q: A streaming job without Streaming Engine was launched with a maximum of 20 workers. Before a campaign the team updates it to allow 60 workers, but it never scales past 20. What is the reason and the fix?
choices: The autoscaler needs a higher latency tier, so the team should raise the tier and update the running job again
Pub/Sub throttles the subscription, so the team should add more subscriptions and split the topic traffic
Disks were allocated at launch for the old maximum, so relaunch higher or move to Streaming Engine
The worker service account lacks a role for scaling, so the team should grant it the Dataflow Admin role
quiz.explain: Without Streaming Engine, Persistent Disks are allocated at launch and an update cannot exceed the original maximum, so the job must be relaunched with a higher value or moved to Streaming Engine. A latency tier only tunes how eagerly Streaming Engine jobs scale up.

days.recap: Dead-letter topics, retention with seek, and one subscription per region cover Pub/Sub failures. Streaming Engine makes scaling flexible; replace jobs with name mappings and fix stuck drains by updating them.

days.title: Streaming II: Windows, Watermarks, Triggers and Write Semantics

concepts.heading: Windows Group an Unbounded Stream by Event Time
concepts.body: A stream has no end, so aggregations need windows: finite pieces cut by element timestamp. Tumbling windows (Beam calls them fixed) are consistent, disjoint intervals, so each element lands in exactly one window; page views per clock hour is the textbook case. Hopping windows (Beam: sliding) have a fixed length and start every period, so they overlap; a five-minute window starting every minute gives a running average refreshed each minute. Session windows hold elements within a gap duration of each other, and data after the gap starts a new window; they are assigned per key, which suits player activity with a ten-minute gap and sessions of very different lengths. Windows use the element's timestamp. If the pipeline assigns arrival or publish time, a backlog delivered after a six-hour outage lands in the current window and produces a spike. Taking the timestamp from the event's own time field puts delayed events where they belong.

concepts.heading: Watermarks, Late Data and Triggers
concepts.body: A watermark is a threshold for when Dataflow expects all data of a window to have arrived, and the data source determines it. An element with a timestamp inside a window that arrives after the watermark passed the window's end is late data. By default a trigger emits a window's result when the watermark passes its end, and late data is dropped. With the Beam SDK you can set an allowed lateness and add triggers on event time, processing time, element counts or combinations. For hourly order counts where mobile clients deliver orders up to 30 minutes late, allow lateness and add a late trigger so the pipeline emits an on-time result and then refined updates. Data later than the allowed lateness is still dropped. The downstream table must expect updates for a window, because a refined result replaces or supplements the earlier one. Windows that stay open for a long time also keep state per key.

concepts.heading: Exactly-Once, At-Least-Once and BigQuery Write Methods
concepts.body: Dataflow streaming jobs run in exactly-once mode by default: records are not dropped or duplicated as they move through the pipeline. At-least-once mode loses no record but may duplicate some, and it can significantly lower cost and latency. It suits map-only work such as log parsing, per-record schema translation of change data, pipelines that deduplicate downstream, and sinks that cannot guarantee exactly-once. Aggregations like counts and sums, and business-critical uses such as fraud detection, stay exactly-once. Match the BigQuery write method to the mode. STORAGE_WRITE_API gives exactly-once semantics; STORAGE_API_AT_LEAST_ONCE has lower latency but allows duplicate writes. STREAMING_INSERTS is the legacy API, still the default for unbounded collections, with best-effort deduplication, and it is not recommended for new projects. FILE_LOADS is incompatible with at-least-once mode. The Dataflow mode and the connector method should tell the same story.

concepts.heading: Bad Records, Hot Keys and Bounded Sources
concepts.body: Streaming Dataflow retries a failing element indefinitely instead of skipping it, so one bad record can stall a job. Plan a dead-letter path: with the Storage Write API, rows that cannot be written are available as a separate collection from the write result, and parse failures can go to a side output. Route both to a table or bucket with the error and the original payload so the main flow continues and engineers can fix and replay them. Another stall is the hot key. In Streaming Engine the buffered input and state for open windows has a documented limit per key, and exceeding it leaves the pipeline stuck with high system lag. One placeholder ID for all anonymous visitors is the classic cause. Salt the key into shards, aggregate partially and combine in a second step. Finally, a file source run with the streaming flag is still bounded and ends when the files are read. For new files, send bucket notifications to Pub/Sub and read that subscription.

examPoints: A question about a running average that refreshes every minute over five minutes points to hopping (sliding) windows, hourly disjoint totals point to tumbling windows, and activity separated by idle gaps points to session windows.
A question about a spike after a delayed backlog, or orders arriving after the window closed, points to event-time timestamps plus allowed lateness and a late trigger.
A question about duplicates versus cost in a map-only job points to at-least-once mode with STORAGE_API_AT_LEAST_ONCE, while exact counts point to exactly-once with STORAGE_WRITE_API.

quiz.q: A pipeline counts web orders per clock hour by event time. Mobile clients buffer orders offline, so some arrive 30 minutes after the hour ends, and the finished counts are too low. What change addresses this?
choices: Switch to session windows with a thirty-minute gap so that every late order extends the open hourly window
Move to at-least-once mode so that the late orders are delivered again and counted on a second attempt
Replace the event timestamps with the arrival times so that every order falls inside the current window
Allow lateness on the window and add a trigger that emits refined results when late orders arrive
quiz.explain: Allowed lateness keeps the window open for late elements and a late trigger emits updated counts. Arrival time would put orders into the wrong hour, and at-least-once mode concerns duplicates, not lateness.

quiz.q: A map-only streaming job parses application logs and writes them to BigQuery, where a view already removes duplicates. The business wants lower cost and latency and accepts occasional duplicate rows. What fits?
choices: Exactly-once mode with the legacy streaming inserts method, because it deduplicates on a best-effort basis
At-least-once mode with the at-least-once Storage Write API method, and the view removes duplicates
At-least-once mode with the batch file loads method, because load jobs are cheaper for continuous data
Exactly-once mode with a Storage Write API stream per worker so that no duplicate rows can be produced
quiz.explain: A map-only pipeline with downstream deduplication is the case at-least-once mode targets, and the matching connector method is the at-least-once Storage Write API. File loads cannot be combined with that mode, and the legacy inserts are not recommended for new projects.

days.recap: Pick windows by shape (tumbling, hopping, session), assign event time, and handle late data with allowed lateness and triggers. Match exactly-once or at-least-once to the BigQuery write method, and add dead-letter paths.

days.title: Batch Processing: Dataproc, Data Fusion, Kafka and Templates

concepts.heading: Dataproc: Separate Storage from Compute
concepts.body: On-premises Hadoop couples storage (HDFS) to the compute nodes, so the cluster must stay up to keep data available. On Google Cloud the usual pattern keeps data in Cloud Storage and treats Dataproc clusters as disposable. The Cloud Storage connector lets Spark and Hive read and write gs:// paths like HDFS, so existing code needs little change. A manufacturer with 300 TB in HDFS and nightly jobs on a cluster idle 18 hours a day copies the data to Cloud Storage, changes paths, and creates a cluster for each run and deletes it afterwards, paying only for the job hours. Dataproc (now branded Managed Service for Apache Spark; the exam guide uses the Dataproc name) offers workflow templates and Cloud Composer operators to create, run and delete clusters automatically. A persistent cluster is justified when many users run interactive work all day.

concepts.heading: Secondary Workers and the BigQuery Connector
concepts.body: A Dataproc cluster has primary workers, which are standard VMs running HDFS DataNodes, and optional secondary workers. Secondary workers only process: they hold no HDFS data, only a local cache. They can be Spot VMs, preemptible VMs or non-preemptible VMs. Because a reclaimed node loses no stored data, Spark can reschedule its tasks, which makes them a cheap way to add peak capacity for fault-tolerant batch jobs. Keep the master and primary workers stable, and keep data in Cloud Storage so even a primary-worker loss is harmless. When a Spark job must read a multi-terabyte BigQuery fact table, use the Spark BigQuery connector. It reads through the BigQuery Storage Read API, which reads the table's data in a distributed manner across executors and it writes results back to BigQuery. A manual export adds a copy, delay and cleanup.

concepts.heading: Cloud Data Fusion and Kafka Integration
concepts.body: Cloud Data Fusion is a managed, code-free integration service built on the open-source CDAP project. Users design pipelines on a canvas by connecting plugins for sources, transforms, aggregates and sinks, and can use Wrangler for interactive cleansing. At run time it provisions an ephemeral Dataproc cluster in your project, runs the pipeline with Spark and deletes the cluster. Choose it when analysts with little programming experience need to pull Oracle tables, join, cleanse and load BigQuery with prebuilt connectors; choose Dataflow or Dataproc when engineers want code-level control. For Apache Kafka, Google provides an Apache Kafka to BigQuery Dataflow template, so no pipeline code is needed (the Google Cloud tutorial runs it against Managed Service for Apache Kafka); a broker in your own data center also needs private connectivity from the workers, such as Cloud VPN or Interconnect. Teams with Kafka client code that must not change can use Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Kafka; new workloads without Kafka ties are usually simpler on Pub/Sub.

concepts.heading: Dataflow Templates: Flex Versus Classic
concepts.body: Templates package a pipeline so that design and deployment are separate: a developer builds it, and a permitted user launches it with parameters from the console, gcloud or the REST API, with no Apache Beam SDK or development environment. They are code artifacts that fit source control and CI/CD, and Google provides open source pre-built templates for common cases. A Flex template packages the pipeline as a Docker image in Artifact Registry plus a specification file in Cloud Storage. On launch, the service starts a launcher VM, pulls the image and builds the execution graph from the runtime parameters. That means it needs no ValueProvider, can choose a different I/O connector by parameter and can validate parameters before the job starts; Google recommends it for new templates. A classic template is the serialized static graph, with runtime parameters wrapped in ValueProvider, which not every source and sink supports.

examPoints: A question about nightly Hadoop or Spark jobs with idle hours and a request for minimal code changes points to data in Cloud Storage with the connector and an ephemeral Dataproc cluster per run.

A question about analysts with little programming experience building batch pipelines points to Cloud Data Fusion, and a question about Kafka events into BigQuery without a custom consumer points to the Dataflow Kafka to BigQuery template.
A question about one reusable template that selects a connector by parameter and validates input before launch points to a Flex template, not a classic template.

quiz.q: A Dataproc cluster runs fault-tolerant nightly Spark jobs, and the team wants cheap extra capacity at the peak without paying for more HDFS storage. What should they add?
choices: A second persistent cluster, so that jobs can be split between the clusters and share the same HDFS blocks
Additional master nodes, so that the scheduler can place more Spark tasks on the existing worker machines
Primary workers backed by larger disks, so the cluster gains both extra storage and extra processing power
Secondary workers on Spot VMs, which only process and hold no HDFS data, so reclaimed nodes lose nothing
quiz.explain: Secondary workers add compute only, and Spot pricing suits batch work that tolerates reclaimed nodes because Spark reschedules tasks. More primary workers would add HDFS storage the team does not want, and extra masters do not add task capacity.

quiz.q: A team wants one reusable Dataflow template whose pipeline picks a different I/O connector depending on a parameter and validates the parameters before the job starts. Which template type fits?
choices: A classic template with every runtime parameter wrapped in a ValueProvider so that values can be read at launch
A Flex template, because its graph is built at launch from the runtime parameters and can be validated first
A classic template stored in Cloud Storage, because a static graph can switch connectors without a new build
A pre-built Google template, because it accepts an unlimited set of connector choices without any custom code
quiz.explain: A Flex template builds the execution graph dynamically at launch, so it can choose connectors by parameter and validate inputs. A classic template is a fixed serialized graph, and pre-built templates cover only their predefined scenarios.

days.recap: Keep batch data in Cloud Storage and run ephemeral Dataproc clusters with Spot secondary workers. Use Data Fusion for code-free pipelines, the Kafka template for brokers, and Flex templates for reusable pipelines.

days.title: BigQuery Transformations, AI Enrichment and Data Acquisition

concepts.heading: Stored Procedures for Reusable SQL Logic
concepts.body: A BigQuery stored procedure is a named, reusable collection of SQL statements saved in a dataset. It accepts IN, OUT and INOUT arguments, can declare variables and use procedural language such as IF, WHILE and RAISE, and callers run it with CALL, including from other datasets they can access. A nightly job that declares a date variable, deletes a partition, inserts recomputed rows, checks the row count and raises an error when it is zero is a natural procedure, and several teams can call the same logic with different arguments. A procedure has no schedule of its own: run it from a scheduled query, Cloud Composer, Workflows or Dataform. SQL procedures execute inside BigQuery; procedures for Apache Spark are a separate type and not what a plain SQL procedure uses. Putting the logic in one place means a fix applies everywhere the procedure is called.

concepts.heading: MERGE for Change Data
concepts.body: BigQuery supports DML, including MERGE, which combines INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE in one statement driven by a join between a source and a target table. It is atomic: all the changes apply or none do. For a nightly staging table that holds a feed of new customers, changed addresses and flagged deletions, one MERGE joins staging to production, uses WHEN MATCHED clauses to update or delete changed keys, and WHEN NOT MATCHED to insert new ones. The alternatives are weaker. Rebuilding the whole table touches every row, separate insert, update and delete statements are not atomic as a group, and appending everything pushes deduplication onto every reader. A MERGE can sit inside a stored procedure, and a single recurring statement with nothing depending on it can run as a BigQuery scheduled query, which is built on BigQuery Data Transfer Service and needs no extra infrastructure.

concepts.heading: Generative AI Enrichment from SQL
concepts.body: BigQuery can call Gemini models from SQL, so unstructured text can be enriched where it already lives. You create a remote model that references a Gemini endpoint through a BigQuery connection, then call AI.GENERATE_TEXT in a query; the scalar AI.GENERATE function can also call Gemini directly without a remote model. Prompt text is built from table columns, inference runs in Google Cloud, and the results are written to a new table. For 5 million support tickets that need a sentiment and a list of topics, this avoids exporting data and needs no labelled training set, because the foundation model follows the prompt. It is plain SQL, so analysts can schedule it. Cost depends on token counts, so test on a sample first. Optimized mode of the managed AI functions is still Preview, so a design should not depend on it.

concepts.heading: Extracting Fields from Files and Choosing How Data Arrives
concepts.body: BigQuery can treat objects in Cloud Storage as ObjectRef values, created with OBJ.MAKE_REF from a URI or taken from an object table. Generative AI functions accept them, so a query can send a scanned PDF to Gemini with a prompt. AI.GENERATE with an output schema returns typed fields such as name, date and amount in a STRUCT that can be stored in columns; AI.GENERATE_TABLE is the table-valued variant over a remote model. A table definition over PDFs exposes only metadata or bytes, and regular expressions cannot read scanned images. Acquisition follows the same smallest-tool rule. A BigQuery subscription loads Pub/Sub messages without code, Datastream captures database changes, scheduled queries and the transfer service move recurring loads, and the Storage Write API serves custom streaming writers. Pick the entry point from the source type and whether any transformation happens on the way.

examPoints: A question about reusable multi-step SQL logic with variables and error handling shared by several teams points to a BigQuery stored procedure called with CALL, scheduled from outside.
A question about applying inserts, updates and deletes from a staging table atomically points to a MERGE statement with WHEN MATCHED and WHEN NOT MATCHED clauses.
A question about labelling millions of rows or extracting fields from PDFs without moving data points to BigQuery remote models and AI.GENERATE functions, with ObjectRef values for files.

quiz.q: Each night a staging table receives new customers, changed addresses and flagged deletions. The engineer must apply all of it to the production table so that either everything is applied or nothing is. What should the engineer use?
choices: Three separate statements run in order: first an INSERT, then an UPDATE and finally a DELETE statement
A scheduled query that rebuilds the whole production table from staging by using CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE
A MERGE statement that joins staging to production, with WHEN MATCHED and WHEN NOT MATCHED clauses
An append-only load of the staging rows into production, with a view that picks the latest row per key
quiz.explain: MERGE applies inserts, updates and deletes from one join in a single atomic statement. Separate statements are not atomic as a group, a rebuild rewrites every row, and append-only pushes deduplication onto each reader.

quiz.q: A claims team has 200,000 scanned PDF forms in Cloud Storage and needs the claimant name, date and amount as typed BigQuery columns, without exporting the files. Which approach fits?
choices: Define an external table over the bucket and parse the PDF content with regular expressions in SQL
Load the PDFs into Bigtable and let the table parse each form into columns using its built-in parser
Reference the files as ObjectRef values and call AI.GENERATE with an output schema for typed fields
Run a daily scheduled query that copies the PDF metadata into a table and splits the file names
quiz.explain: ObjectRef values let a query send each document to Gemini, and an output schema returns typed fields that can be stored. An external table exposes only metadata or raw bytes, and regular expressions cannot read scanned images.

days.recap: Reusable SQL goes in stored procedures, atomic change data in MERGE, simple schedules in scheduled queries. Enrich text and files with Gemini from SQL, and pick the entry point from the source and the transformation.

days.title: Deployment and Operation: Cloud Composer, Workflows and CI/CD

concepts.heading: Match the Orchestrator to the Complexity
concepts.body: Scheduling choices form a ladder, and operations effort and idle cost grow with each rung. A single recurring SQL statement fits a BigQuery scheduled query. A few dependent SQL steps fit Dataform workflow configurations or a stored procedure called by a scheduled query. Calls across services without Airflow needs fit Workflows, triggered by Cloud Scheduler. Many dependent tasks across services with retries and backfills fit Cloud Composer. Workflows is a serverless orchestrator: steps in YAML or JSON call HTTP endpoints and Google Cloud connectors, branch, loop, retry, wait for callbacks and keep state, with no charge while idle. Cloud Composer (now Managed Service for Apache Airflow; the exam guide uses Cloud Composer) runs DAGs with a large operator library, schedules and backfills on an environment with a baseline cost. Existing Airflow code or dozens of dependent tasks favor Composer; light API glue favors Workflows.

concepts.heading: Workflows: Connectors and Retries
concepts.body: A connector is a built-in wrapper around a Google Cloud API such as BigQuery, Dataflow, Cloud Run or Dataproc. Compared with a raw HTTP call it handles authentication with the workflow's service account, applies retry behavior for transient errors and, for long-running operations, waits for completion, so the author writes no polling loop or job-ID handling. Use http.get or http.post only for APIs without a connector, such as third-party services, and add your own retry and wait logic. For a flaky external API that occasionally returns 503, wrap the call in a try step with a retry policy: a predicate for transient errors, such as the built-in http.default_retry covering 429, 502, 503 and 504, a maximum number of attempts and an exponential backoff. Backoff gives the service time to recover and avoids retry storms. Moving to Composer does not remove the need to define retries.

concepts.heading: Composer Operations: Sensors, Triggers, Cleanup and Secrets
concepts.body: These are Airflow features: the Composer docs cover the triggerer setting and the Airflow REST API, while sensor modes and trigger rules come from the Airflow documentation. A sensor is an Airflow task that waits for a condition such as a file in Cloud Storage. In the default poke mode it holds a worker slot for the whole wait, so many sensors on a busy morning can starve other tasks. A deferrable sensor hands the wait to the triggerer, an asynchronous component, so the task frees its slot until the condition is met; the environment needs its number of triggerers set above zero. Reschedule mode also frees the slot between checks. For events, a Cloud Storage object finalize event can invoke a Cloud Run function that calls the environment's Airflow REST API to start a DAG run (the Composer docs link to a guide on triggering DAGs with Cloud Run functions). Cleanup tasks need the all_done trigger rule: the default all_success skips the delete-cluster task when the Spark job fails and leaves a Dataproc cluster running. Move passwords and keys out of source control by configuring Secret Manager as the Airflow secrets backend.

concepts.heading: CI/CD for Pipelines
concepts.body: Treat pipeline code like application code: Git, review, automated tests and a repeatable release. A Composer environment reads DAGs from the dags folder of a Cloud Storage bucket it owns, and the Composer test guide has you try DAGs in a separate test location or environment first. The Composer CI/CD guide page could not be retrieved, so the following flow is a common practice rather than a documented recipe: run automated DAG tests in a build service such as Cloud Build when a pull request opens, then copy reviewed files into the production environment's dags folder after merge. Editing production files directly bypasses review. For Dataform, a release configuration compiles a chosen Git branch or tag into a compilation result, and a workflow configuration executes it on a cron schedule with a chosen service account, so only reviewed code on the production branch runs each morning. For Dataflow Flex Templates, Cloud Build runs tests, builds the container image into Artifact Registry with a version tag, and creates the specification file in Cloud Storage. Other projects then launch from the spec, and versioned images give rollback.

examPoints: A question about chaining HTTP calls and connectors, waiting for a callback and paying nothing while idle points to Workflows, while backfills, existing Airflow DAGs or dozens of dependent data tasks point to Cloud Composer.
A question about DAG sensors starving worker slots points to deferrable sensors, and a cleanup task skipped after a failure points to the all_done trigger rule.

A question about production runs from reviewed code points to CI with Cloud Build, a Dataform release plus workflow configuration, or a Flex Template image in Artifact Registry with a spec in Cloud Storage.

quiz.q: A finance analyst needs a single MERGE statement to run every night at 02:00. Nothing depends on it and no other tasks need coordination. Which option fits best?
choices: A BigQuery scheduled query that runs the statement on a schedule, with no infrastructure to maintain
A Workflows definition triggered by Cloud Scheduler that calls the BigQuery API with the statement
A Dataproc workflow template that starts a cluster, runs the statement through Spark and then deletes it
A Cloud Composer environment with a DAG that runs the statement on a nightly schedule at 02:00
quiz.explain: One recurring statement belongs on the lowest rung of the ladder: a scheduled query needs nothing else. Composer and Workflows can run it, but they add an environment or definition to maintain for no benefit, and Dataproc is unrelated to a SQL statement.

quiz.q: A DAG creates a Dataproc cluster, runs a Spark job and deletes the cluster. When the job fails, the delete task is skipped and the cluster keeps running. What is the best fix?
choices: Run a weekly cleanup DAG that lists and deletes any cluster created by the pipeline in the past week
Switch the sensor tasks to deferrable mode so that the failed job releases its worker slot and the cluster
Increase the retries on the Spark job task so that the failing job eventually succeeds and the DAG continues
Set the delete task's trigger rule to all_done so that it runs whether the job task succeeded or failed
quiz.explain: The default all_success rule skips a task whose upstream failed, whereas all_done runs it after upstream tasks finish in any state. More retries hide real bugs, and a weekly sweep still leaves up to a week of cost.

days.recap: Use the lowest rung that fits: scheduled query, Dataform, Workflows, then Composer. Free worker slots with deferrable sensors, clean up with all_done, keep secrets in Secret Manager, and release through CI.

days.title: Selecting Storage Systems: Bigtable, Spanner, AlloyDB, Cloud SQL, Firestore, Memorystore and Cloud Storage

concepts.heading: Start From the Access Pattern, Not the Product
concepts.body: Storage questions are won by naming the access pattern first: how data is read and written, how fast, how consistent, and how large it will grow. Analytical scans over many rows belong in BigQuery. Single-row lookups and range scans at very high throughput point to Bigtable. Relational transactions point to Cloud SQL, AlloyDB or Spanner, depending on scale and geography. Nested documents synced to mobile apps point to Firestore, and sub-millisecond reads of data that can be rebuilt point to Memorystore. Files and raw objects go to Cloud Storage. Bigtable is a wide-column NoSQL store with consistently low latency that scales by adding nodes; you read by row key or by a contiguous key range, so the row key design decides performance. A key that starts with a timestamp piles every new write onto one node, while a key that starts with a device or user identifier spreads writes and still keeps one entity's rows together. A fleet of sensors writing millions of readings per second and read back by sensor and time range is the textbook Bigtable case. Ad hoc SQL joins across tables are not.

concepts.heading: Choosing Among Spanner, AlloyDB and Cloud SQL
concepts.body: The three relational services differ in how far a single primary can take you. Cloud SQL runs managed MySQL, PostgreSQL or SQL Server with automated backups, point-in-time recovery, a standby in another zone for high availability and read replicas. It fits regional, moderate-size applications that need engine compatibility and little change. AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is PostgreSQL-compatible with higher transactional performance and a columnar engine that speeds analytical queries on live operational data, plus read pool instances that move reporting off the primary. It fits an order system whose managers run heavy aggregate reports during the day and slow order entry. Spanner is the choice when writes must scale out horizontally or when the application needs strongly consistent, externally consistent transactions across regions, as a global payments ledger does. Its multi-region configurations replicate with automatic failover. The trap is over-engineering: a 200 GB regional HR application on Spanner pays for global scale it will never use, and one that needs only moderate scale rarely needs a redesign for it.

concepts.heading: Firestore and Memorystore: Documents and the Speed Layer
concepts.body: Two services serve application needs that the data engineer must still recognise. Firestore is a serverless document database: data lives in documents inside collections, and documents can hold subcollections, so a note with its comments maps naturally. Its mobile and web SDKs provide real-time listeners that push changes to clients and offline persistence that syncs on reconnect, which is why a startup building a collaborative app picks it. It is not a warehouse; heavy analytics still go to BigQuery. Memorystore is a managed in-memory store offering Valkey, Redis and Memcached engines. Because data sits in memory, reads and writes complete in sub-millisecond time, which suits caching, session stores, rate limiting and real-time leaderboards built on sorted sets. The design rule is that Memorystore complements a durable system of record rather than replacing it: when a gaming company keeps player profiles in a relational database and needs a leaderboard read tens of thousands of times a second, the cache sits in front, and anything in it can be rebuilt from the database.

concepts.heading: Cloud Storage Classes, Lifecycle Rules and Autoclass
concepts.body: Cloud Storage holds raw files, exports and archives, and cost is shaped by storage class. Standard suits frequently read data. Nearline, Coldline and Archive are progressively colder: lower storage cost, but retrieval fees and a minimum storage duration, so deleting or moving an object early still charges for the remainder. Choose the coldest class whose minimum duration fits the object's expected life and whose retrieval cost fits how often it is read. Two features change classes automatically. Object Lifecycle Management applies rules you write, usually on object age, and is the precise tool when the pattern is predictable: audit exports read daily at first, rarely in the next year, then kept for compliance move down on a schedule and are deleted at the end. Autoclass moves each object from its own access history, returning read objects to Standard, which suits unpredictable access such as a genomics lab reopening runs at random. A bucket cannot combine Autoclass with lifecycle rules that set storage class, so the choice is either-or for class transitions.

examPoints: A question about billions of time-stamped readings with millisecond key lookups and no joins points to Bigtable, with a row key that spreads writes and groups one entity.

A question that needs strongly consistent SQL transactions across continents points to Spanner, while PostgreSQL plus fast reporting on live data points to AlloyDB and a modest regional application points to Cloud SQL.
A question about Cloud Storage cost with a predictable age pattern points to lifecycle rules, and with unpredictable access it points to Autoclass.

quiz.q: A bank keeps payment-audit exports in Cloud Storage. Dashboards read them daily for a month, investigators open them rarely during the next year, and after that they are kept only for compliance until deletion. Which approach fits best?
choices: Enable Autoclass on the bucket and rely on it to pick the cheapest class for each object
Add lifecycle rules that move objects to colder classes by age and delete them at the end
Store every export in Archive class from the start so the storage rate is as low as possible
Keep everything in Standard class and review a monthly report of the objects nobody has opened
quiz.explain: The pattern follows object age, so lifecycle rules by age are the exact tool. Autoclass is tempting because it is automatic, but it reacts to access and cannot be combined with class-setting lifecycle rules, and starting in Archive would make the daily dashboard reads expensive.

quiz.q: An order-entry application runs on PostgreSQL. Managers run heavy aggregate reports on the live data all day, which slows order entry. The team wants to keep PostgreSQL compatibility and speed up the reports without a separate warehouse. Which choice fits?
choices: Move the application to Spanner so that the database scales its writes across several regions
Move the application to Bigtable and rewrite the reports as scans over contiguous row key ranges
Place Memorystore in front of the database so that every report is served from memory
Move to AlloyDB and use its columnar engine and read pool instances for reports
quiz.explain: AlloyDB keeps PostgreSQL compatibility, accelerates analytical queries on operational data with its columnar engine and offloads reads to read pool instances. Spanner is tempting for scale, but the problem is mixed workloads, not global writes, and it would need design changes.

days.recap: Name the access pattern first: Bigtable for key lookups at scale, Spanner for global consistent SQL, AlloyDB for PostgreSQL plus analytics, Cloud SQL for regional OLTP, Firestore for documents, Memorystore as a cache. For Cloud Storage, lifecycle rules suit predictable age patterns and Autoclass suits unpredictable access.

days.title: Designing the BigQuery Warehouse: Partitioning, Clustering and Schema Shape

concepts.heading: Choosing the Partition Column and Granularity
concepts.body: Partitioning splits a table into segments so a query that filters on the partitioning column reads only the matching ones. BigQuery partitions by a time-unit column (DATE, TIMESTAMP or DATETIME), by ingestion time, or by an integer range. The question to ask is which column analysts actually filter on. Devices that upload up to a week late make ingestion-time partitioning misleading: a reading from Monday that arrives on Friday sits in Friday's partition, so event-date queries read the wrong segments. Partitioning on the event timestamp column puts each row in the day it belongs to. When the natural filter is an integer such as a region identifier, integer-range partitioning takes a start, an end and an interval. Granularity matters too: daily partitions suit large daily volumes over a limited span, while a small amount of data per day across many years, or backfills that touch a wide range of dates, favours monthly or yearly partitions combined with clustering on the date column to keep pruning fine-grained. Partitions also enable partition-level expiration for retention.

concepts.heading: Clustering: Column Order, Existing Data and Cost Estimates
concepts.body: Clustering sorts the data inside storage blocks by up to several chosen columns, in the order you list them, so queries that filter or aggregate on those columns read fewer blocks. Order matters: the first column is the primary sort, so list columns in the order of how often and how strongly they are filtered, starting with the one used most. Clustering combines well with partitioning: partition by order date, cluster by status and country. Two behaviours surprise learners. First, adding clustering to an existing table does not recluster old rows; only newly written data is organised, so to get benefit on history you rewrite the data, for example by creating a clustered copy with a CREATE TABLE AS SELECT. Second, the number of blocks a clustered query reads is known only when it runs, so a dry run or a maximum-bytes-billed check uses an upper-bound estimate, and a query on a clustered but unpartitioned table can be rejected although its real cost would be within the limit. Partitions give exact pre-run estimates.

concepts.heading: Guardrails: Require a Partition Filter and Retention
concepts.body: Partitioning saves money only when queries use the partition column, and teams forget the filter. The table option to require a partition filter makes BigQuery reject any query on the table that does not include a predicate on the partitioning column, so an analyst cannot accidentally scan fifteen terabytes. It can be set at creation or added later. Retention is the other guardrail. Partition expiration deletes each partition once its partition time is older than the setting, calculated per partition, and leaves the table in place with its schema and permissions, which is what a rolling window of recent raw events needs. Table expiration, by contrast, deletes the whole table, and a dataset default applies only to tables created after it is set. For history the business still needs at lower detail, aggregate the rows into a summary table and let expiration remove the detail. When a defect is found after the recovery window has passed, scheduled table snapshots preserve a point in time cheaply because only changed bytes are billed beyond the base table.

concepts.heading: Denormalization, Nested Fields and When Star Schemas Are Fine
concepts.body: Joins force BigQuery to move data between workers, and normalized storage savings matter little in a columnar warehouse, so Google recommends denormalizing. The recommendation is specific: use nested and repeated fields (STRUCT and ARRAY) rather than flattening completely.
