An order with its lines stored as an array of structs inside one row keeps the parent and its children together, so reading them needs no shuffle, and parent columns are not repeated on every line as they would be in a flat table. This fits data that is always read together, such as orders and their lines. The recommendation has limits. A well-tuned star schema, with a fact table and small shared dimensions, is already efficient for analytics, and folding every dimension into a billions-row fact table adds storage and makes a dimension change touch every row. The exam rewards matching the shape to the access: hierarchical data read together is nested, shared dimensions that change independently can stay as separate tables.

examPoints: A question about late-arriving device data queried by event time points to partitioning on the event timestamp column, not ingestion time.
A question about analysts accidentally scanning an entire partitioned table points to the require-partition-filter option, and a rolling retention window points to partition expiration.
A question about an order and its lines always read together points to nested and repeated fields, while an existing well-tuned star schema points to leaving it alone.

quiz.q: A ride-sharing company loads trip events from devices that sometimes upload data a week late. Analysts always filter on the device-recorded event timestamp. How should the BigQuery table be partitioned?
choices: By the event timestamp column, so each late row lands in its own event day
By ingestion time, so that each load job writes to a single partition for the day it ran
By an integer range on the trip identifier, so that late rows fill in the older ranges
By no partitioning at all, with clustering on the event timestamp to prune by block
quiz.explain: Time-unit column partitioning puts each row into the partition of its own value, so event-date filters prune correctly even for late data. Ingestion-time partitioning is tempting because it needs no column, but a row that arrives a week late would sit in the wrong partition.

quiz.q: An e-commerce team keeps orders, order_lines and shipments in three tables. Analysts almost always read an order together with its lines, and lines are never queried alone. What schema change does BigQuery guidance favour?
choices: Split the lines into one table per month so that every join is limited to a small slice
Flatten orders and lines into one wide table that repeats the order columns on every line row
Store the lines as a repeated STRUCT field inside orders so they are read in one row
Add a clustered index on the order identifier in both tables so that the join becomes a lookup
quiz.explain: Nested and repeated fields keep parent and children in one row, so no shuffle is needed and parent columns are not duplicated. Full flattening is tempting but repeats the order columns on every line, and flattening gives up the benefit of keeping children in the parent row.

days.recap: Partition on the column analysts filter by, pick granularity to the data volume, and cluster in filter order; clustering is not applied to old rows. Require a partition filter and use partition expiration as guardrails. Nest data read together; leave a good star schema alone.

days.title: Data Lake on Google Cloud: BigLake, Open Formats and Cost Control

concepts.heading: BigLake Tables and Access Delegation
concepts.body: A data lake keeps open-format files such as Parquet in Cloud Storage and still has to be governed. BigLake tables let BigQuery query that data in place with access delegation: a connection backed by a service account reads the files, and users are granted access to the table only, never to the bucket. This is what lets a retailer give analysts SQL access to Parquet files without handing them storage permissions. Because users go through the table, BigQuery can enforce row-level and column-level security on files that stay in open formats, and for Cloud Storage tables also dynamic data masking. Other engines benefit too: Spark, Hive and Trino can read BigLake tables through BigQuery connectors, and the Storage API applies the same row and column policies on that access. The trade-off is that the data is still external. BigLake adds governance and multi-engine access to the lake; it does not turn the files into native BigQuery storage, with its automatic storage optimisation and the performance that follows.

concepts.heading: Layout and Metadata Caching for Large Lakes
concepts.body: Query planning over object storage can be slower than the query itself. With millions of files, a BigLake table must list objects to find what to read, and that listing can take minutes. Two design decisions help. First, lay files out with Hive-style partition folders such as dt=2026-11-06/region=EU/, and declare those keys as partition columns, so a filter on them skips whole folders instead of opening every file; a flat folder forces every query to touch every file. Second, enable metadata caching, which stores file names, partitioning information and physical metadata such as row counts so queries skip the listing and prune faster. Refresh can be automatic, at a system-chosen interval, or manual, which suits pipeline output that changes at known times. The maximum staleness setting says how old the cache may be for a query to use it; when the cache is older, the query falls back to reading source metadata and is slower. Caching helps most with many files and Hive partition filters.

concepts.heading: Iceberg and the Limits of Caching
concepts.body: Open table formats change where metadata lives. Apache Iceberg tables carry their own metadata: manifest files record the data files and their statistics, and BigQuery reads that directly. So metadata caching is not used with Iceberg external tables and would add nothing; a question that proposes caching for an Iceberg table is offering a distractor. The same reasoning places caching where file discovery is the cost: BigLake tables and object tables with many files. Matching the table form to the work is part of lake design. A related decision is lake versus warehouse storage. Querying open-format data in place suits very large, rarely queried history and data that other engines also read. Data queried constantly by hundreds of dashboard refreshes is better in native BigQuery storage with partitioning and clustering, so a common design keeps cold history in the lake and loads the hot, recent slice into native tables. Cached metadata narrows the gap for external files but does not close it.

concepts.heading: Discovery and Cost Control in the Lake
concepts.body: A lake that nobody can search turns into a swamp. Dataplex Catalog, documented today as Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog, with API and IAM names unchanged), indexes technical metadata for Cloud Storage, BigQuery and other sources, so one search covers many projects, and results are limited to what the searcher is allowed to see. Cost control is the other half. Lifecycle rules on landing buckets delete or downgrade raw files by age, but note soft delete: by default a deleted object remains recoverable and is still stored, and billed, for the soft delete retention duration, so a retention rule shows up on the bill with a lag; shortening that bucket setting reduces the lag. Store and layout choices cut query cost too, because partition folders reduce bytes read. Finance asking why the bucket shrinks later than the 30-day rule suggests is a soft-delete question, not a failure of the lifecycle rule.

examPoints: A question about analysts querying Parquet in Cloud Storage with row and column security and no bucket access points to BigLake tables with access delegation.
A question about queries that spend minutes listing millions of files in Hive-partitioned folders points to BigLake metadata caching, and an Iceberg table is the case where caching does not apply.
A question about hot dashboard data over a 400 TB open-format lake points to loading the hot slice into native BigQuery tables, keeping history in the lake.

quiz.q: A BigLake table points to a Cloud Storage prefix holding several million Parquet files in Hive-style partition folders. Filtering on the partition folders still makes queries spend minutes listing objects. What should the data engineer do?
choices: Enable metadata caching on the table so file and partition information is cached
Convert the BigLake table to a view so that BigQuery stops reading the object metadata
Grant analysts storage viewer on the bucket so that they can list the files themselves
Add a reservation of dedicated slots so that the object listing is processed faster
quiz.explain: Metadata caching stores file names, partitioning information and physical metadata, so the query skips the object listing. Extra slots are tempting for slow queries, but listing objects in the external store is not slot work.

quiz.q: A lake team keeps an Apache Iceberg table in Cloud Storage, queried from BigQuery as an Iceberg external table. A colleague wants metadata caching to speed up query planning. What is the best response?
choices: Enable it with automatic refresh, because caching always shortens planning for external tables
Enable it with manual refresh, because Iceberg manifests are rewritten only by the pipeline
Do not enable it, because Iceberg manifests already hold the file metadata
Enable it only after moving the Iceberg files into a flat folder with one directory
quiz.explain: Iceberg tables carry their own metadata in manifest files and BigQuery reads it directly, so the cache is not used with Iceberg external tables. Manual refresh sounds careful but changes nothing, since the cache does not apply here.

days.recap: BigLake gives governed, multi-engine access to open-format files through access delegation. Lay files out in Hive partition folders and use metadata caching for many-file tables, but not for Iceberg. Keep cold history in the lake, hot data in native tables, and remember soft delete when judging lifecycle savings.

days.title: Data Platform and Governance: Dataplex Catalog, Data Products, Quality and Lineage

concepts.heading: The Catalog: Entries, Aspects and Entry Groups
concepts.body: Governance starts with knowing what data exists. Dataplex Catalog, which current documentation calls Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog; API, CLI and IAM names did not change), automatically indexes technical metadata from Google Cloud sources such as BigQuery, Cloud Storage and Cloud SQL, so one search box covers many projects. Search results respect the source permissions of the person searching. For sources it does not index, such as an on-premises Oracle database, stewards register custom entries. The model has four parts. An entry represents a data asset. An aspect type defines the schema of structured metadata, such as owner, sensitivity and retention. An aspect is an instance of that type attached to an entry or column. An entry type is a template that can require specific aspects, which is how a steward guarantees nobody registers an entry without an owner and a retention class. An entry group is a regional container for entries and the administrative boundary: set view or edit permissions on the group once, and they apply to every entry inside.

concepts.heading: Data Products and Federated Governance
concepts.body: A data mesh treats data as a product: the domain that understands the data owns and publishes it, while a central function sets shared standards. That is federated governance, in contrast with centralized (consistent but a bottleneck) and decentralized (fast but inconsistent). In Google Cloud terms the central team defines the policy tag taxonomy, Sensitive Data Protection settings and catalog standards, while domain teams classify their own columns and curate their own data. Data products in the catalog package related assets such as BigQuery tables and views into one curated unit that consumers can discover and evaluate. Access groups map friendly roles to Google Groups or service accounts, so consumers request access through the product rather than emailing the owner, and contracts record what the owner promises, such as the refresh schedule and quality standards. A retailer whose sales, logistics and finance teams want others to find and request their data without waiting on a central team is describing exactly this.

concepts.heading: Classification and Business Meaning: Policy Tags and Glossaries
concepts.body: Two pieces turn raw columns into governed data. Policy tags in a taxonomy classify BigQuery columns, and access control on a tag then applies to every column carrying it. Google's guidance is to define a small number of data classes and apply one tag to many columns. A hierarchy helps: High, Medium and Low sensitivity parents with leaf tags such as credit card or government ID let an administrator grant access on a tier once to cover all its leaves. For a bank with hundreds of tables across eight domains, this scales where per-column grants do not. The business glossary handles meaning rather than access. It organises glossaries, categories and terms, and a definition link connects a term such as Net revenue to the physical columns that implement it, so searching the term finds the right columns and shows the agreed definition. A text file in a bucket cannot be searched or linked to a column, which is why a glossary in the catalog beats it.

concepts.heading: Quality, Profiling and Lineage
concepts.body: Three catalog-connected capabilities answer the questions a steward gets asked. Auto data quality validates BigQuery tables against rules, such as non-null order IDs, on a schedule or on demand; rules belong to dimensions like completeness, results produce scores, and scans can be incremental, checking only new rows by a date or timestamp column, which suits a daily load. Results can be published into the catalog so consumers see table health where they discover it. A data profile scan computes column statistics such as null percentage, distinct values and common values, which helps when you must write rules for a 300-column table you did not design; rule recommendations from a profile can be a starting point, so the typical flow is profile first, then adopt rules, then schedule quality scans. Data lineage records where data originates, how it changes and where it goes. Before dropping a column, a platform team needs downstream impact, several levels deep, and lineage provides that traversal where single-level lookups would miss indirect dependents.

examPoints: A question about analysts who cannot find which tables hold customer orders across 60 projects points to Dataplex Catalog search, scoped by the searcher's permissions.
A question about domain teams publishing curated data with self-service access requests and a refresh promise points to data products with access groups and contracts under federated governance.
A question about writing quality rules for a table nobody understands points to a data profile scan first, and about the impact of dropping a column points to data lineage.

quiz.q: A team must write data quality rules for a 300-column BigQuery table that it did not design and understands poorly. It wants null percentages, value distributions and common values to base the rules on. What should it run first?
choices: An auto data quality scan with rules for every column written from guesses about the data
A data profile scan on the table, then adopt recommended rules for scheduled quality scans
A data lineage query on the table, then copy the rules from the upstream source tables
A policy tag taxonomy review on the table, then derive the rules from the sensitivity tiers
quiz.explain: A profile scan computes the column statistics, and its recommendations are a starting point for quality rules. Writing rules from guesses is tempting because quality scans are the end goal, but they check explicit rules and do not discover what the data looks like.

quiz.q: The owner of a source table plans to drop a column. The platform team must know which downstream tables and reports depend on it, several levels deep, before approving. Which capability answers that?
choices: Auto data quality scores, which report which downstream tables fail rules after a change
Entry group permissions, which list every team that currently holds access to the table
Business glossary links, which show every report that mentions the column's business term
Data lineage, which records downstream dependencies for multi-level impact checks
quiz.explain: Lineage records how data flows between assets, so a downstream traversal shows every dependent several levels deep. The glossary is tempting because it links terms to columns, but it records meaning, not data flow.

days.recap: Catalog entries, aspects and entry groups organise metadata and admin boundaries. Data products with access groups and contracts deliver federated governance. Policy tags classify at scale, the glossary defines meaning, profiling informs quality rules, and lineage answers impact questions.

days.title: Preparing Data for Visualization: BI Engine, Materialized Views and Column Security

concepts.heading: BI Engine for Dashboards
concepts.body: BI Engine is an in-memory analysis layer that speeds BigQuery SQL for dashboards. It works through the BigQuery API, so Looker and other BI tools need no change, it uses a vectorized runtime and caches only the queried parts of columns and partitions, and it works with authorized views, column-level security and data masking. You reserve memory capacity per project and region, and can name preferred tables so only the data dashboards use is loaded; partitioning by time means only recent partitions occupy memory. The best fit is a large fact table joined to small dimensions, or pre-aggregated native tables. BI Engine has documented exclusions: external tables including BigLake tables, JavaScript UDFs and remote functions, JSON and RANGE types, row-level security, search and vector search, recursive queries and BigQuery ML queries. Unsupported stages fall back to normal slots without failing. When dashboards sit on a BigLake table and show no acceleration, the documented workaround is to write the query result to a native table, refreshed on a schedule that matches how stale the data may be.

concepts.heading: Materialized Views and Precalculated Fields
concepts.body: A materialized view precomputes and stores query results, and BigQuery keeps it current. For a limited SQL surface, incremental materialized views add only new rows to the cached result, so a dashboard repeating the same aggregation by country and day over an events table that gets inserts all day reads current numbers at lower cost than rerunning the query or a scheduled full refresh. Smart tuning goes further: if part of a query against a base table can be answered by an incremental materialized view, BigQuery reroutes it automatically, so developers need not change their queries, much like an index. A caveat: if the source team starts running UPDATE and DELETE on historical base rows, incremental updates are no longer possible, BigQuery falls back to the original query, and the view stops helping until it refreshes. The broader principle is to precalculate expensive or business-critical fields, such as lifetime value or a churn flag, in the pipeline, for example with Dataform, so the cost is paid once per load and every dashboard shares one definition.

concepts.heading: Diagnosing a Slow Query
concepts.body: Query execution details separate a badly shaped query from a busy platform. If a join stage outputs far more rows than it receives, the key is probably not unique or the join is many-to-many; the fix is to reduce data before the join by filtering or aggregating, or to correct the key. If the timeline shows few active units while many stay queued, the query is waiting for slots rather than being inefficient, a contention symptom. Under on-demand pricing, queries share a pool; capacity-based pricing with reservations provides dedicated slots. Query performance insights surface findings such as slot contention, insufficient shuffle quota, high-cardinality joins and partition skew, each with guidance. Notice what BigQuery does not have: no worker nodes to rebalance, no manual statistics to refresh and no B-tree indexes to tune, so options that propose these are distractors. A report that normally takes 40 seconds and today takes minutes with a low active count and a high queued count is a contention question, not a rewrite question.

concepts.heading: Column Security, Masking and Sensitive Data Discovery
concepts.body: Dashboards often meet data that only some people may see in full. Column-level security attaches a policy tag to a column; a user without the Fine-Grained Reader role on the tag cannot read it, and a SELECT * returns an error that lists columns to exclude. Dynamic data masking sits on top: a data policy maps a masking rule to a policy tag and to principals holding the Masked Reader role, so their existing queries keep working and receive masked values. Choose the rule by what the user must still do. Nullify hides the value and is useless in a join. A default masking value returns a constant per data type. SHA-256 hashing returns a type-preserving hash, which is right when analysts must join two tables on email to count repeat buyers without seeing addresses, because the same input always gives the same output. When a company does not know where personal data sits across 300 projects, Sensitive Data Protection discovery profiles resources continuously, classifies columns into infoTypes and reports sensitivity and risk.

examPoints: A question about dashboards on a large native fact table that must respond in seconds points to BI Engine, and one on a BigLake table points to writing results to a native table first.
A question about a repeated aggregation that must always be current at the lowest cost points to an incremental materialized view, not a scheduled query that reruns in full.
A question about analysts joining on a column they must not see in clear points to hash masking, while queries breaking on a protected column point to dynamic data masking.

quiz.q: A team reserved BI Engine capacity, but dashboards on a BigLake table over Parquet files in Cloud Storage show no acceleration. The dashboards can tolerate data that is a few hours old. What should the team do?
choices: Increase the BI Engine reservation until the external table fits entirely in memory
Mark the BigLake table as a preferred table so that BI Engine accelerates it in place
Write the query result into a native table on a schedule and point the dashboards at it
Switch the dashboards to a view over the BigLake table so that BI Engine can treat it as native
quiz.explain: BI Engine does not accelerate external tables, including BigLake tables, so a scheduled native table is the documented workaround when some staleness is acceptable. A larger reservation is tempting, but the limit is the table type, not memory.

quiz.q: Analysts must join an orders table to a customer table on the email column to count repeat buyers, but must not see actual addresses. The join must still work across both tables. Which masking rule fits?
choices: Nullify, which returns NULL in the column so that both the value and its data type are hidden
Default masking value, which returns one constant per data type for every row
Hash with SHA-256, which gives a type-preserving value that is identical for identical input
Last four characters, which shows only the final four characters of each stored address
quiz.explain: Hashing gives the same output for the same input, so joins still match while the address stays hidden. Nullify is tempting for hiding data but produces NULL everywhere, which breaks the join.

days.recap: BI Engine accelerates native tables for dashboards, not external ones. Incremental materialized views keep repeated aggregations cheap and current, but base updates and deletes weaken them. Read execution details to tell bad joins from slot contention, and use policy tags with hash masking when users must join but not see.

days.title: Preparing Data for AI and ML: BigQuery ML, Features and Embeddings

concepts.heading: BigQuery ML and Feature Preprocessing
concepts.body: BigQuery ML lets people who know SQL create, evaluate and run models with GoogleSQL, and the models live in datasets next to the tables, so 80 million rows of customer data never leave the warehouse. That is the answer when analysts with SQL skills but no Python want to predict churn. Features still need preparation. BigQuery ML performs some preprocessing automatically during training, such as handling categorical and numeric columns, and offers manual preprocessing through the TRANSFORM clause of CREATE MODEL, with functions like bucketizing and feature crossing. The advantage of TRANSFORM is that the transformation is stored with the model and applied automatically in ML.EVALUATE and ML.PREDICT, so callers send raw columns. Without it, a team that scales and buckets features in the training query but sends raw rows at prediction time creates training-serving skew: the model sees different distributions in production than it learned from, and good evaluation scores turn into poor live predictions.

concepts.heading: Splits, Leakage and Trustworthy Evaluation
concepts.body: A model can look excellent in evaluation and fail in production because of how the data was prepared. Data leakage happens when a training feature contains information that will not exist when the prediction is made. If a demand forecast uses the average discount of the very week being predicted, the model effectively sees the answer; evaluation looks superb, while production has no such value. The fix is to build features only from what is known at prediction time, such as discounts planned or past sales. Splits matter as well. For time-dependent data, evaluation rows should come after training rows. A random split scatters weeks of the same trend into both sets, so neighbouring rows leak across and the evaluation overstates quality. Splitting by time, with training on the earlier period and evaluation on the later one, mimics real use. In a data engineer's role, these are data preparation duties: the right grain, the right label, the right cut-off date and a split that matches how the model will be used.

concepts.heading: Embeddings, Vector Search and Exact versus Approximate
concepts.body: An embedding is a vector that places similar content close together, so semantic matching works where exact keys fail. A bank matching '12 Main St.' with '12 Main Street' across three customer systems can embed the address text and use vector search to find near-duplicates for entity resolution. VECTOR_SEARCH compares a query embedding with the vectors in a table. Without a vector index it measures distance to every record, so results are exact. With a vector index, created with CREATE VECTOR INDEX, it uses approximate nearest neighbor search, which is faster on large tables but can miss true neighbors. So pick exact search for modest tables where a miss is costly, such as 150,000 contract clauses searched a few times a day, and approximate for millions of items under latency or batch-window pressure. A pre-filter narrows candidates, and it prunes data only when the filter uses partitioned columns or stored columns of the index, so partitioning a ticket table by date lets a last-30-days search read far less.

concepts.heading: Data Preparation for RAG and Embedding Model Changes
concepts.body: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a model in your own documents. In BigQuery the flow is to parse the documents, generate embeddings, optionally create a vector index, run VECTOR_SEARCH with the question's embedding and pass the best matches to a Gemini model as context. The key preparation step is chunking. An embedding is one vector for the text it was given, so a whole 80-page policy blurs many topics into one point and retrieval returns vague matches; splitting into passages of coherent size gives each topic its own vector and gives the model focused context. A second lifecycle point: embeddings from different models, or different versions of a model, live in separate embedding spaces and are generally incompatible even when dimensions match. When Google retires an embedding model, regenerate the stored embeddings with the replacement, change any query-time embedding generation to the same model, and rebuild the vector index. Mixing old and new vectors gives inaccurate search results.

examPoints: A question about SQL analysts building a churn model without moving data points to BigQuery ML, with the TRANSFORM clause when preprocessing must be applied at prediction time.
A question about excellent evaluation and poor production predictions points to leakage or a random split on time-ordered data, or to training-serving skew.

A question about preparing documents for retrieval-augmented generation points to chunking before embedding, and a retired embedding model points to regenerating all embeddings and rebuilding the index.

quiz.q: A churn model built in BigQuery ML scored well in evaluation but predicts poorly in production, where requests arrive as raw rows. The training query had computed scaled and bucketed features in SQL. What is the best fix?
choices: Retrain with a larger dataset, so that the model sees more variation in the scaled columns
Move the model to a bigger reservation, so that the predictions run with more dedicated slots
Rebuild the model with those transformations in the TRANSFORM clause and send raw columns
Add a vector index on the feature columns so that prediction retrieves similar customers
quiz.explain: Putting preprocessing in TRANSFORM stores it with the model and applies it automatically in evaluation and prediction, which removes the skew. More data is tempting for poor results, but the problem is that training and serving see different feature distributions.

quiz.q: An insurer wants an assistant that answers questions from 20,000 long policy PDFs. A data engineer prepares the corpus in BigQuery for retrieval-augmented generation. Which preparation step improves retrieval most?
choices: Embed each whole document as a single vector so that each policy has exactly one entry
Split the documents into coherent passages and generate an embedding for each passage
Create a vector index first and delay chunking until the assistant returns poor matches
Hash every document with SHA-256 and search the hashes for the question text
quiz.explain: Chunking gives each topic its own vector, so retrieval returns focused passages for the model. One vector per document is tempting for simplicity, but it blends many topics into one point and returns vague matches.

days.recap: BigQuery ML keeps SQL modelling inside the warehouse; use TRANSFORM to avoid training-serving skew and split time-ordered data by time to avoid leakage. VECTOR_SEARCH is exact without an index and approximate with one. For RAG, chunk before embedding, and regenerate all embeddings when the model changes.

days.title: Sharing Data: Authorized Views and Datasets, and BigQuery Sharing (Analytics Hub)

concepts.heading: Authorized Views: Share Answers, Not Tables
concepts.body: A view is a virtual table defined by a query, and normally a user querying it also needs access to the tables it reads. An authorized view removes that need: the view is authorized on the source dataset, so it reads the source data on behalf of the analysts. Analysts get access only to the dataset holding the view and can query its rows and columns, but cannot read the underlying tables. A finance table with customer names, account numbers and monthly totals can then expose just regional monthly totals to regional analysts. The view's SQL is the contract: it chooses the columns and filters the rows. An expensive aggregation shared with 300 internal analysts and refreshed through the day can be an authorized materialized view, which gives the same access control with cached, precomputed results. The common failure is a trap: a view that analysts are merely told to use enforces nothing if they also hold Data Viewer on the base table, because they can query the base table directly.

concepts.heading: Authorized Datasets and Fine-Grained Controls
concepts.body: Authorizing views one at a time does not scale. A reporting dataset with 35 views, and new ones each week, would need 35 authorizations and more every week. An authorized dataset authorizes all views in a dataset to read a second dataset: the dataset holding the views is the authorized dataset, the dataset they read is the source, and principals are given access to the view dataset. New views are covered automatically. Sharing can also be finer than datasets. Row-level access policies filter rows with a predicate and a grantee list, and column-level security with policy tags controls specific columns, so one table can serve several audiences from a single copy of the data. When a publisher shares one large orders table and each partner must see only its own sales region, a row-level policy per partner keeps one table to maintain, whereas copies per partner multiply storage and risk of drift. These controls are evaluated against the identity of the caller at query time.

concepts.heading: BigQuery Sharing (Analytics Hub): Publish and Subscribe Across Organizations
concepts.body: For sharing across projects and organizations, the exam guide's Analytics Hub, shown in current documentation as BigQuery sharing, is a publish and subscribe service that shares without replicating data. A publisher places a shared dataset into a listing inside a data exchange and controls who may subscribe. A subscriber who subscribes gets a linked dataset in its own project: a read-only reference to the publisher's data, not a copy, so there is nothing to refresh and the subscriber can query it in real time. The subscriber pays for its own queries, and the publisher pays for storage. A weather-data company serving 40 customer organizations needs this, not 40 copies or 40 export jobs. Exchanges are private by default; a public exchange or public listing is discoverable by all Google Cloud users, so a supplier that must restrict discovery to three partners keeps them private and shares with specific users or groups. Roles separate duties: Admin creates exchanges and grants access, Publisher publishes listings, Subscriber subscribes, Viewer browses.

concepts.heading: Controlling Egress, and Sharing Streams
concepts.body: Sharing raises a second question: what can subscribers do with the data? A subscriber could copy shared tables into its own project with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT or exports, defeating the provider's licence. A publisher can set data egress restrictions on a listing, on query results, or both. When they apply, copy, clone, export and snapshot options are unavailable, BigQuery Data Transfer Service is unavailable on the restricted dataset, and writing query results to a destination table or view is blocked. Subscribers can still query the data in place. Sharing is not limited to tables. Pub/Sub topics can be listed in an exchange as shared topics, and a subscriber receives a linked Pub/Sub subscription in its own project, so two partner companies can receive the same vehicle telemetry in near real time without the publisher copying messages or managing separate subscriptions per partner. The exam decision is to pick the sharing mechanism that keeps one copy under the owner's control.

examPoints: A question about analysts who may query totals but not read the underlying names and accounts points to an authorized view, and a growing number of views points to an authorized dataset.
A question about sharing a live curated dataset with dozens of external organizations without copies points to BigQuery sharing (Analytics Hub) with a listing and linked datasets.
A question about subscribers copying licensed shared tables points to egress restrictions on the listing, and about streaming the same events to partners points to a shared Pub/Sub topic.

quiz.q: A finance dataset has a table with customer names, account numbers and monthly totals. Regional analysts must query only the monthly totals by region and must not be able to read the underlying personal columns. Which approach fits?
choices: Create a view of the totals, authorize it on the source and give analysts access to its dataset
Create a view of the totals and give analysts Data Viewer on the source dataset so it can run
Copy the totals into a new table each night and give analysts Data Owner on that copy
Export the totals to Cloud Storage and give analysts the storage viewer role on the exported file
quiz.explain: An authorized view reads the source on behalf of analysts who have no access to the base table. Giving Data Viewer on the source is tempting because the view needs data, but it lets analysts query the personal columns directly.

quiz.q: A weather-data company wants about 40 customer companies, each in its own Google Cloud organization, to read a continuously updated curated BigQuery dataset. The company does not want to create copies or run export jobs. What should it use?
choices: A scheduled query that writes the dataset into each customer's project every hour
A data exchange listing of the dataset, which each customer subscribes to
An authorized dataset in each customer's project that points back at the company tables
A Cloud Storage export on a schedule with a signed link sent to each customer
quiz.explain: A listing in a data exchange lets each subscriber receive a linked dataset, a read-only reference to the live data with no copies. A scheduled query to each project is tempting, but it creates copies that must be refreshed and paid for 40 times.

days.recap: Authorized views share answers instead of tables, and an authorized dataset covers many views at once. Row-level policies and policy tags give one table many audiences. BigQuery sharing (Analytics Hub) publishes listings that subscribers read as linked datasets; egress restrictions block copying, and shared topics stream events to partners.

days.title: Optimizing Resources: Cost per Business Need, Ephemeral Clusters and Critical-Job Availability

concepts.heading: Match the cost model to the business need
concepts.body: Optimizing resources starts with asking what the business needs from a workload, not with the cheapest setting. A nightly report that nobody watches tolerates delay and can run on cheap, interruptible capacity. A dashboard that executives open at nine o'clock needs fast, predictable answers and justifies reserved capacity. BigQuery shows the split clearly. With on-demand pricing you are charged for the bytes a query processes, not for rows returned or time taken, so one unfiltered query over a wide table can dominate a month. Custom daily quotas per project or per user are a hard cap: once reached, queries stop. A dry run reports the bytes a query would process before it runs, so analysts can fix column lists and filters first. Capacity pricing instead bills slots and lets an administrator cap a reservation. Neither is better in general: bursty, small and unpredictable workloads often suit on-demand, while steady heavy workloads suit capacity. State the need, then choose.

concepts.heading: Persistent versus job-based (ephemeral) Dataproc clusters
concepts.body: Dataproc clusters are quick to create and bill while they run. When data lives outside the cluster, in Cloud Storage and BigQuery rather than on HDFS, compute can be disposable. A media company that runs a nightly Spark job on a cluster idle for twenty hours a day should create a cluster for the run and delete it afterwards, with the same Spark code. A workflow template with a managed cluster does exactly this: it creates the cluster, runs a graph of jobs and deletes the cluster when the workflow ends. Cloud Composer can drive the same pattern for richer orchestration. Ephemeral clusters are also easier to size, because each runs one workload. A persistent cluster still has a place when many users submit ad hoc work at unpredictable times. Even then, cluster scheduled deletion removes a cluster after an idle period, at a fixed time or after a set duration, so forgotten clusters stop billing. Idle time counts from when no jobs are running. (Docs now show Dataproc as Managed Service for Apache Spark.)

concepts.heading: Cheaper workers and autoscaling without surprises
concepts.body: Dataproc has primary and secondary workers. Secondary workers can be Spot VMs, preemptible VMs or non-preemptible VMs, and they hold no HDFS data, so they add compute cheaply. Keep them below half of all workers, expect more single-task failures and raise retry limits, because savings are not guaranteed when preemptions lengthen jobs. Short batch jobs fit best. An autoscaling policy sets boundaries, frequency and aggressiveness. It suits clusters that keep data in Cloud Storage or BigQuery and clusters that handle many jobs. It is not the tool for shrinking an idle cluster to a minimum, since creating a cluster is about as fast as resizing one: delete idle clusters instead. It is also not recommended for on-cluster HDFS, because HDFS utilization is not a scaling signal, and it does not support Spark Structured Streaming. Scale-down uses graceful decommissioning, so one eight-hour job delays the release of workers that small jobs no longer need. Group similar-sized jobs together and give each long job its own cluster.

concepts.heading: Dataflow FlexRS and availability for critical jobs
concepts.body: Cost and availability pull in different directions, and the data engineer chooses per job. Flexible Resource Scheduling (FlexRS) lowers the cost of autoscaled batch Dataflow pipelines by using advanced scheduling, the Dataflow Shuffle service and a mix of preemptible and regular VMs. The price is a scheduling delay, because Dataflow queues the job and starts it within six hours of creation, so it fits non-urgent work such as a weekly re-index that may run any time in a twelve-hour window. It does not support GPUs or Compute Engine reservations. A critical job needs the opposite: capacity it can count on. For a nightly Dataproc workflow that fails at creation because one zone lacks the requested machines, omit the zone and let Auto Zone pick one in the region. Auto Zone prefers a zone covered by your resource reservations, plus on-demand capacity when needed, and otherwise the zone most likely to satisfy the request. Dependence on a single named zone is the weakness. Reservations and Auto Zone together protect the critical run, while FlexRS and Spot workers belong to the tolerant ones.

examPoints: A question where a cluster sits idle most of the day and all data is in Cloud Storage or BigQuery points to an ephemeral cluster created by a workflow template, and a question about forgotten ad hoc clusters points to scheduled deletion after an idle period.

A question about a batch Dataflow job that can finish anywhere inside a long window points to FlexRS, and one about a nightly cluster failing for lack of machines in one zone points to omitting the zone so Auto Zone chooses.
A question about one analyst's unfiltered query inflating an on-demand bill points to custom daily quotas and dry runs, not to a bigger cluster or a different file format.

quiz.q: A retailer runs a recurring Spark batch ETL on Dataproc. Input and output are in Cloud Storage, the job tolerates the occasional slow task, and the team wants lower compute cost without rewriting code. Which change fits best?
choices: Move the input to HDFS on the workers, because local disks make every task faster and so shorten the billed time
Add secondary workers on Spot VMs, kept below half of all workers, and raise the task retry limits for failures
Replace the primary workers with preemptible VMs only, because they hold no HDFS data and the job needs none
Turn on autoscaling with a minimum of two workers, because the policy removes all cost while the cluster is idle
quiz.explain: Secondary workers add cheap compute that holds no HDFS data, and keeping them below half of the workers with higher retry limits absorbs preemptions. A cluster made only of preemptible primaries is not supported advice, and autoscaling to a minimum still bills the idle cluster.

quiz.q: A weekly Dataflow batch pipeline rebuilds a product index. It may run at any time in a twelve-hour window on Sunday, and finance wants the lowest worker cost. Which option should the data engineer enable?
choices: Dataflow Prime with GPU workers attached, because accelerators finish the job sooner and so lower the billed hours
Compute Engine reservations for the workers, because reserved machines always run faster than flexible ones do
Flexible Resource Scheduling, which accepts a delayed start and mixes preemptible and regular VMs for batch work
A streaming job that runs all week, because spreading the work thinly keeps each worker small and cheap
quiz.explain: FlexRS trades a scheduling delay for lower cost on autoscaled batch jobs, and a twelve-hour window tolerates the delay. Reservations and GPUs are not supported with it and raise cost, and a week-long streaming job keeps paying for workers.

days.recap: State the business need first, then pick the model: ephemeral job-based Dataproc clusters when data is external, scheduled deletion for ad hoc ones, Spot secondary workers and FlexRS for tolerant batch work, and Auto Zone with reservations for critical runs.

days.title: Automation and Repeatability, DAG Design, BigQuery Editions, Slots and Reservations

concepts.heading: Choosing the scheduler: Cloud Scheduler, Workflows or Cloud Composer
concepts.body: Three tools cover most scheduling. Cloud Scheduler is a managed cron service: it starts something on a schedule but does not model steps or dependencies. Workflows is a serverless orchestrator for sequences of service and HTTP calls, with retries, conditions and waiting on long-running operations; a Cloud Scheduler job can trigger it. Cloud Composer, the managed Apache Airflow service (docs now name it Managed Service for Apache Airflow), fits data pipelines with many dependent tasks, backfills, sensors and Python-defined DAGs, but it is an always-on environment you pay for and operate. Take a nightly job that calls a partner REST API, waits for a Cloud Run job, runs one BigQuery statement and sends a notification: a short chain of service calls is a Workflows case, and standing up Composer for it is more than the job needs. For a single recurring SQL statement, a BigQuery scheduled query is enough. It is built on BigQuery Data Transfer Service, and the docs warn that a query set exactly on the hour might trigger more than once, so schedule at 08:58 or 09:03 and make the statement safe to repeat.

concepts.heading: Designing DAGs that can be re-run
concepts.body: A DAG is a graph of tasks with dependencies, and Composer guidance says each task should be an idempotent unit of work: running it twice leaves the same end state. An append-only load adds the day again on every re-run. Loading into the partition for the run date with overwrite, or using MERGE on a key, is idempotent, and using the run's logical date instead of the wall clock makes a re-run hit the same data. Do not bury a multi-step workflow in one PythonOperator, because separate tasks can be retried, monitored and alerted on individually and show where a run stopped. Airflow pools cap concurrent tasks for a shared resource, so three hundred fan-out tasks calling one partner API can share ten slots without slowing unrelated tasks. A task that needs its own Python dependencies can use PythonVirtualenvOperator, and KubernetesPodOperator runs a task in its own pod (GKE operators can target a separate cluster). Finally, DAG files are parsed repeatedly, which is why start_date should be a fixed date, not a dynamic one.

concepts.heading: BigQuery Editions, reservations and assignments
concepts.body: On-demand bills TiB processed, so bills swing with occasional huge queries. Capacity-based pricing, BigQuery Editions, bills slot-hours through reservations, and you can use both models together. The three editions (Standard, Enterprise, Enterprise Plus) differ in capabilities, availability target and compute model. You choose one when creating a reservation, and to change it you delete and recreate the reservation, so plan from requirements. Standard edition reservations cannot set baseline slots. A reservation has a baseline, always allocated and always billed, and an optional autoscaling maximum, billed while scaled. An assignment links a project, folder or organization (folders and organizations are not available to Standard reservations) to a reservation. It takes effect only if the reservation has non-zero baseline, non-zero autoscaling slots, or is set to use idle slots and some are free. Otherwise the message says the assignment is pending and the project runs as on-demand, shown by a NULL reservation_id in INFORMATION_SCHEMA. Size the baseline for steady load and let autoscaling cover peaks, since baseline sized for the worst peak wastes money.

concepts.heading: Idle slots, interactive versus batch jobs, and commitments
concepts.body: Slots unused by one reservation are shared by default with others in the same administration project. The documentation warns not to rely only on idle slots for production work with strict timing: they can be taken back at any time, and a reservation with no baseline and no autoscaling then pauses or queues queries. Setting ignore_idle_slots only stops that reservation from borrowing, so it does not help by itself. Give time-critical work baseline or autoscaled slots. Jobs are interactive by default and start as soon as possible. Batch jobs have lower priority and are more likely to queue when compute is fully used, so scans, reports and backfills with no human waiting should run as batch instead of competing with dashboards. Separate reservations per workload, assigned at project level, isolate them entirely. For a planned heavy event, autoscaling draws on available capacity and may be delayed in high demand, so raise baseline well ahead of time. A capacity commitment gives a discount for steady use and cannot be reduced during its term, so commit only to the floor, for example a flat 1,000 slots, and autoscale the rest.

examPoints: A question where tasks must be re-run safely or a scheduled INSERT created duplicate rows points to idempotent design: partition overwrite or MERGE, a logical date, and an off-the-hour schedule.
A question about a short chain of API and service calls on a schedule points to Cloud Scheduler with Workflows, while many dependent data tasks with backfills point to Cloud Composer.

A question where a project assigned to a reservation still runs as on-demand (NULL reservation_id) points to a reservation with no baseline, no autoscaling and no idle slots, and one about changing an edition points to deleting and recreating the reservation.

quiz.q: A Cloud Composer DAG loads one day of sales into BigQuery with an append task. Operators often re-run failed days from the Airflow UI, and the table now has duplicate rows. What change makes re-runs safe?
choices: Disable task retries and require operators to confirm each run, so no day can ever be loaded twice
Merge extract, load and notify into one Python task, so the whole day either succeeds or fails together as one
Overwrite the run date's partition using the logical date, so every repeat of the load gives one result
Schedule the DAG to start every day exactly on the hour, because that time is protected against repeated triggers
quiz.explain: An idempotent load, overwriting the partition for the logical date or merging on a key, leaves the same end state however often it runs. Disabling retries removes resilience without stopping manual re-runs, and one big task makes failures harder to locate.

quiz.q: An admin assigns a new ETL project to a reservation that has zero baseline, no autoscaling slots and idle slot use disabled. The project's jobs still show a NULL reservation_id. What is the cause and the fix?
choices: The assignment is pending and jobs run on demand, so add baseline or autoscaling slots, or allow idle slot use
The project is too small for a reservation, so the admin should assign its parent folder to the reservation instead
The edition does not match the project, so the admin should switch the reservation's edition in place and retry
The jobs are batch priority, so the admin should mark them interactive and the reservation id will then be filled in
quiz.explain: An assignment needs a reservation that has baseline, autoscaling slots, or idle slots it may use; otherwise the project runs as on-demand with no reservation id. Priority does not decide it, and an edition cannot be switched in place anyway.

days.recap: Pick the lightest orchestrator that fits, make every task and scheduled query idempotent, and size BigQuery reservations with baseline for steady load, autoscaling for peaks, batch priority for patient work and commitments only for the floor.

days.title: Monitoring and Troubleshooting: Cloud Monitoring, Cloud Logging, INFORMATION_SCHEMA, Quotas and Billing

concepts.heading: Alerting on pipeline health with Cloud Monitoring
concepts.body: Dataflow publishes job metrics to Cloud Monitoring, so you can chart them and create alerting policies. For a streaming job feeding a live dashboard, alert on system lag, the maximum lag across the pipeline in seconds, to learn that the pipeline is falling behind. To detect a failed pipeline, alert on the failed metric, which is set to 1 when a job exits with a failure. The job status value is an enum and cannot be charted or used for alerts. Element count and byte count are per PCollection, so they are not job-level alerting signals. Cloud Composer follows the same idea at platform level: a liveness DAG named airflow_monitoring runs on a schedule and feeds the composer.googleapis.com/environment/healthy metric, true on success and false on failure, so alert on that. Setting email_on_failure in a DAG sends nothing unless the environment is configured with an email service such as SendGrid or SMTP, and task mail would not show an unhealthy platform anyway. A metric alert answers 'is the number wrong'; choose it when the signal is numeric.

concepts.heading: Cloud Logging: log-based alerts and Dataflow errors
concepts.body: When the signal is text rather than a number, use Cloud Logging. A log-based alerting policy notifies whenever a specified message appears in included logs, such as a particular error string in Dataproc driver output or an audit log record; you define the matching query and channels with no custom parser. Uptime checks test endpoint reachability, and billing export holds cost, so neither fits. Logs also explain failures. Dataflow retries a whole bundle when an element throws. In batch, a bundle that fails four times fails the pipeline, so a job that dies after an hour of work usually hit one bad record repeatedly. In streaming the bundle is retried indefinitely and the pipeline stalls instead of failing. The fix is data handling: catch the exception in the DoFn and send the element to a dead-letter output in Cloud Storage or BigQuery. The log entry 'Processing stuck in step' points to code that is deadlocked, stuck or extremely slow, or to a hanging external call. Expand the entry for a stack trace, and profile with Cloud Profiler if nothing shows.

concepts.heading: BigQuery INFORMATION_SCHEMA for jobs and reservations
concepts.body: BigQuery exposes its own metadata through INFORMATION_SCHEMA views, queried per region. The JOBS views describe every query, load, export and copy job, with fields such as user_email, total_bytes_billed, total_slot_ms and reservation_id. JOBS_BY_USER shows only the caller's jobs. JOBS_BY_PROJECT shows all jobs in the project and requires the bigquery.jobs.listAll permission, which BigQuery Resource Viewer includes; organization-level views span projects. History covers running jobs plus the past 180 days. A platform admin asking which users ran the most expensive queries in the past two weeks sums total_bytes_billed by user_email. A null reservation_id means the job did not run under a reservation. To judge whether a dashboards reservation is well sized, use JOBS_TIMELINE, which splits activity into time slices with slot usage, and compare it with the reservation's capacity, filtering by reservation_id. For script jobs a parent reports its children's usage too, so exclude it with statement_type != 'SCRIPT' to avoid double counting. Job-level slot sums will not match an autoscaling bill, because autoscaled slots are billed as scaled, not as used.

concepts.heading: Quotas, rate limits and cost visibility
concepts.body: Two BigQuery errors look alike but need different action. jobRateLimitExceeded means a job was created but hit a rate limit; use exponential backoff to reduce the request rate and retry with a new job ID. quotaExceeded (HTTP 403) means a project, custom or free-tier quota was exceeded or billing is missing, and that needs the quota or billing fixed rather than retries. For cost, Cloud Billing export to BigQuery writes detailed data through the day, including services, SKUs, projects, labels, locations, cost, usage and credits, so SQL can show what drove a rise. Budgets with threshold rules email recipients when actual or forecast cost crosses a percentage, but an alerts-only budget warns and does not stop usage, and a quota limits usage without guaranteeing spend stops. Together these form the monitoring loop: metrics page people, logs explain, INFORMATION_SCHEMA attributes usage, and billing export attributes money. Pick the source that holds the evidence the question names.

examPoints: A question about a streaming pipeline falling behind or a job that failed points to a Cloud Monitoring alert on Dataflow system lag or the failed metric, while one that needs a page for specific log text points to a log-based alerting policy.
A question where a batch job fails after an hour on one malformed record points to bundle retries and a dead-letter output, and a 'stuck in step' log entry points to slow or hung user code.

A question asking who ran the costliest queries or whether a reservation is well sized points to INFORMATION_SCHEMA JOBS and JOBS_TIMELINE, and one about rising spend by SKU points to Cloud Billing export to BigQuery.

quiz.q: A security team wants an on-call page whenever a specific error message appears in the logs of a Dataproc job. The message has no numeric value. Which monitoring setup meets this?
choices: An uptime check on the cluster's master node, set to notify when the check fails repeatedly over several minutes
A budget with threshold rules on the project, set to notify when forecast spend passes a chosen percentage
A metrics-based alert on Dataflow system lag, set to notify when the maximum lag passes a chosen number of seconds
A log-based alerting policy that matches the error text in the job's logs and notifies the on-call channel
quiz.explain: A log-based alerting policy notifies whenever a matching entry appears, with no custom parser. Uptime checks test reachability, budgets track cost, and Dataflow system lag belongs to a different service and signal.

quiz.q: A pipeline submits hundreds of BigQuery jobs in short bursts, and some fail with jobRateLimitExceeded. Project quotas and billing are healthy. What is the documented way to handle this?
choices: Raise the project's custom daily quota, because this error appears only after the daily byte quota is used up
Use exponential backoff to cut the request rate and retry each failed job under a new job ID
Retry each failed job immediately under its original job ID, because the first attempt was never created
Switch the project from on-demand pricing to a reservation, because the error is only returned to on-demand users
quiz.explain: The job was created and then failed on a rate limit, so slow down with backoff and resubmit with a new job ID. A quota error is a different case, and the pricing model does not decide the rate limit.

days.recap: Use metric alerts for numbers, log-based alerts for text, INFORMATION_SCHEMA for who used what, billing export for money, and treat rate limits with backoff while quota errors need a quota or billing fix.

days.title: Failures and Mitigation: Restarts, Replay, Replication, Failover and Recovery of Bad Data

concepts.heading: Restarting and stopping jobs safely
concepts.body: Dataproc jobs do not restart automatically on failure by default. You can opt in by setting a maximum number of failures per hour (up to 10) and a maximum number of total failures (up to 240), which mitigates out-of-memory errors and unexpected VM reboots and suits long-running and streaming jobs. A job is reported failed if the driver exits non-zero more than four times in ten minutes, or exceeds the limits. Design jobs to restart gracefully: output directories may already exist, and a Spark streaming job that checkpoints can resume. For Dataflow, stopping is a choice. Drain applies only to streaming pipelines: the service finishes buffered and in-flight data and stops ingesting new data, then ends, which suits planned shutdown or replacement that cannot be done by update. Cancel stops immediately, including buffered data, applies to streaming and batch, and a cancelled job cannot be restarted (without Flex Templates it can be cloned). Force cancel is only for a job stuck in cancelling. Pub/Sub keeps unacknowledged messages, so a stopped consumer can pick up again. Draining a Pub/Sub pipeline is the right way to retire it without losing data.

concepts.heading: Replaying data and fixing wrong output
concepts.body: A streaming defect that wrote wrong values for two hours is a fault in processing, not in the infrastructure, and the cure is replay. Once a subscriber acknowledges a Pub/Sub message it becomes inaccessible, but the seek feature alters acknowledgement state in bulk, so you can replay acknowledged messages by seeking to a timestamp or a snapshot, provided the subscription or topic retains them. Fix the pipeline first, then seek back to before the defect. A replay processes some messages a second time, so the sink must be idempotent: a keyed upsert, MERGE or partition overwrite lets corrected rows replace the wrong ones, whereas an append-only sink piles correct rows on top of wrong ones. Dataflow snapshots of a streaming job complement this by saving its state. The same thinking applies to batch: if loads are idempotent, recovery is a re-run. Corruption is not a failover problem, because replicas and standbys faithfully copy a bad write. Only an earlier state helps, so every store needs a way back in time.

concepts.heading: High availability versus disaster recovery, and caches
concepts.body: Match the mechanism to the failure scope. A Cloud SQL high availability instance, called regional, has a primary and a standby in different zones of one region and fails over automatically if the primary becomes unresponsive. After failover the new primary stays primary, and the old one is recreated as the standby; failback returns it to the original zone. The standby cannot serve reads, so use read replicas for that. HA protects against zone or instance failure but not a regional outage, where the HA instance is unavailable too. For that, Google's DR guidance is a cross-region read replica that you promote. Replication is asynchronous, so a little recent data may be lost and RPO is not zero. Corruption or a bad delete needs backups and point-in-time recovery. Memorystore for Redis Standard Tier replicates asynchronously to replicas and fails over automatically, so writes acknowledged by the primary but not yet replicated can be lost, and it does not support cross-region replication. Treat it as a cache, and keep authoritative data, or the events to rebuild it, in a durable store such as Cloud SQL or Bigtable.

concepts.heading: Multi-cluster Bigtable and recovering BigQuery data
concepts.body: Bigtable replication copies data between the clusters of one instance, and each app profile decides how requests are routed. Single-cluster routing sends everything to one named cluster; if it becomes unavailable, you must fail over manually by pointing the app profile at another cluster. Multi-cluster routing sends each request to the nearest available cluster, so failover is automatic when a cluster becomes unavailable. Single-cluster routing gives read-your-writes consistency and a predictable serving cluster, while multi-cluster routing favors automatic availability, so choose by whether the application can tolerate eventual consistency. For BigQuery, time travel keeps changed or deleted data for a window of seven days by default, configurable from two to seven days. You can query a table as of an earlier time, restore a deleted table or dataset, or restore a table to a point in time. Fail-safe adds a non-configurable seven days after the window for emergency recovery at table level. Table snapshots are read-only copies you create yourself, which persist until removed or expired. A faulty UPDATE three days ago is inside the default window and recoverable.

examPoints: A question about retiring a streaming Dataflow job without losing buffered data points to drain, and one about a job that died on a worker reboot points to Dataproc job restart settings and checkpointing.

A question where a standby or replica already contains the dropped table or wrong values points to point-in-time recovery, time travel or snapshots, and wrong streaming output points to Pub/Sub seek plus an idempotent sink.

A question about surviving the loss of a whole region points to a cross-region replica to promote, not a zonal HA instance or Memorystore Standard Tier, and Bigtable automatic failover points to multi-cluster routing.

quiz.q: A team is retiring a streaming Dataflow pipeline that reads from Pub/Sub. It must finish processing data already read and buffered, and no accepted data may be lost. Which action should the engineer take?
choices: Cancel the job, because cancel finishes all buffered data before stopping and can later restart the same job
Force cancel the job, because that is the normal way to stop a healthy pipeline without leaving work behind
Update the job to a new empty pipeline, because an update always discards unfinished buffered work cleanly
Drain the job, so the service finishes buffered and in-flight work, stops ingesting new data and then ends
quiz.explain: Drain is the streaming-only stop that completes in-flight and buffered data first. Cancel drops buffered data immediately and cannot be restarted, and force cancel is reserved for a job stuck in cancelling.

quiz.q: Three days ago a faulty UPDATE overwrote a column across a BigQuery table in a dataset that uses default settings. The team wants the original values back with the least effort. What should they do?
choices: Restore from a manual export, because only an export taken beforehand can bring back overwritten values
Contact support for fail-safe recovery, because deleted data is only reachable once the time travel window has passed
Query or restore the table as of a time before the UPDATE with time travel, which defaults to seven days
Rebuild the table from the source system, because BigQuery keeps no earlier version of changed rows at all
quiz.explain: Three days is inside the default seven-day time travel window, so the table can be queried or restored as of a point before the faulty statement. Fail-safe starts only after that window, and no export is required.

days.recap: Match the mechanism to the failure: restart settings and drain for jobs, Pub/Sub seek with idempotent sinks for bad output, HA for zones, cross-region replicas for regions, multi-cluster routing for Bigtable, and time travel, snapshots or PITR when the data itself is wrong.

days.title: Final Review: Decision Cheat-Sheet Across the Five Domains and Test Day

concepts.heading: Exam format and how to read a data question
concepts.body: The Professional Data Engineer exam lasts 2 hours and has 40-50 multiple choice and multiple select questions. The pass mark is not published, so aim for solid command of every section: designing data processing systems about 22%, ingesting and processing the data about 25%, storing the data about 20%, preparing and using data for analysis about 15%, and maintaining and automating data workloads about 18%. The questions test the engineer's choice, which pipeline, store, model or governance design fits and why, against stated requirements: latency, volume, cost, governance, residency and operational effort. Commands matter little. Read the last sentence first, then underline the decisive constraint, such as 'without changing code', 'lowest operations', 'near real time', 'must not lose data' or 'data may not leave the region'. Each wrong option usually breaks one stated constraint, so mark the hard requirements and discard what breaks them. When nothing forbids it, prefer the managed service. Use the exam guide's product names, and expect docs to show newer ones such as Knowledge Catalog for Dataplex Catalog.

concepts.heading: Cheat-sheet: designing and ingesting (D1, D2)
concepts.body: Security and residency: IAM for who, organization policy for what may be configured, CMEK when the customer must hold the key, Sensitive Data Protection to find and de-identify sensitive fields, and dataset location for residency. Migration: BigQuery Data Transfer Service for scheduled loads from SaaS and other warehouses, Database Migration Service to move a database, Datastream for change data capture from a source that stays live, Transfer Appliance when bandwidth is too small. Streaming: Pub/Sub decouples producers and consumers, with dead-letter topics and ordering keys when needed. Dataflow (Apache Beam) handles windows, triggers, watermarks and late data, and exactly-once processing needs a sink that supports it. Batch Spark or Hadoop code to keep: Dataproc. No-code integration: Cloud Data Fusion. SQL transformations in BigQuery: Dataform or scheduled queries. Orchestration: Cloud Scheduler for a trigger, Workflows for short service-call chains, Cloud Composer for dependent data DAGs with backfills. Cloud Composer is the managed Apache Airflow service; Dataflow templates package a pipeline for repeated launches.

concepts.heading: Cheat-sheet: storing and using data (D3, D4)
concepts.body: Pick the store from the access pattern. Analytics over large data with SQL: BigQuery, using partitioning to prune by date and clustering to prune by common filters. Very high-throughput, low-latency key lookups and time series: Bigtable. Global relational consistency and horizontal scale: Spanner. Familiar relational engines at moderate scale: Cloud SQL or AlloyDB. Documents for apps: Firestore. Cache: Memorystore. Raw files and lake storage: Cloud Storage with lifecycle rules for classes; BigLake and open table formats let several engines read the same data under one set of access policies. Governance and discovery: Dataplex with its catalog for metadata, lineage and data quality. For analysis: BI Engine accelerates dashboard queries, materialized views precompute repeated aggregations, column-level security and data masking protect sensitive fields, and authorized views or datasets share a slice without granting access to the base tables. Analytics Hub (docs now say BigQuery sharing) publishes datasets to other organizations. BigQuery ML trains and runs models in SQL where the data already sits, and embeddings with vector search support retrieval for generative AI.

concepts.heading: Cheat-sheet: maintaining and automating (D5)
concepts.body: Cost: ephemeral job-based Dataproc clusters when data is external, scheduled deletion for ad hoc clusters, Spot secondary workers and FlexRS for tolerant batch, custom quotas and dry runs for on-demand BigQuery. Capacity: reservations with baseline for steady load, autoscaling for peaks, batch priority for patient jobs, commitments for the floor only. Repeatability: idempotent tasks, partition overwrite or MERGE, logical dates, pools to cap concurrency. Monitoring: Cloud Monitoring alerts for numeric signals such as Dataflow system lag, log-based alerts for text, INFORMATION_SCHEMA for job and slot attribution, billing export plus budgets for spend. Errors: backoff and a new job ID for rate limits, a quota or billing fix for quota errors, a dead-letter output for bad records. Failure scope decides recovery: job restarts and drain for jobs, Pub/Sub seek plus an idempotent sink for bad streaming output, HA for zone failure, cross-region replica for region loss, multi-cluster routing for automatic Bigtable failover, and time travel, snapshots or point-in-time recovery when the data is wrong, because replicas copy mistakes.

examPoints: A question that stresses key lookups at very high throughput points to Bigtable, SQL analytics over huge data points to BigQuery, and global relational consistency points to Spanner.
A question that says 'keep the existing Spark code' points to Dataproc, 'serverless stream or batch with Beam' points to Dataflow, and 'dependent tasks with backfills' points to Cloud Composer.

A question where replicas already hold the damage points to time travel, snapshots or point-in-time recovery, and one that fixes a region-wide outage points to a cross-region design, not zonal high availability.

quiz.q: A company needs to serve single-digit-millisecond lookups on billions of device readings keyed by device and time, with throughput that grows steadily. Analysts will separately run SQL over the history. Which pairing fits?
choices: Cloud SQL for the serving lookups, with the same instance used for the analysts' large SQL queries over history
Memorystore for the full history of readings, with exports to Cloud Storage that analysts open with spreadsheets
Firestore for the readings, with each analyst running the long scans directly against the live collections
Bigtable for the serving lookups, with the data also made available to BigQuery for the analysts' SQL
quiz.explain: Bigtable is built for high-throughput, low-latency key access and time series, and BigQuery serves large SQL analysis. A single relational instance, a cache or a document database does not scale to both patterns.

quiz.q: A data engineer must run a nightly chain of dependent tasks with backfills across Dataproc, BigQuery and a partner API, retrying and alerting on each step. Which service fits best?
choices: Cloud Scheduler alone, because a cron trigger models every dependency and retry between the separate steps
A BigQuery scheduled query, because it can start the Dataproc job and call the partner API in one statement
Dataflow streaming, because a continuous pipeline replaces the need to order and retry the nightly steps
Cloud Composer, because DAGs model dependencies, retries and backfills with monitoring for each task
quiz.explain: Composer runs Airflow DAGs, which model dependent tasks, per-task retries and alerts, and backfills. Cloud Scheduler only starts something on a schedule, and a scheduled query runs SQL, not a Dataproc and API chain.

days.recap: Read for the decisive constraint, choose the managed service that meets it, pick stores by access pattern, orchestrators by dependency depth, and recovery by failure scope, remembering that replicas copy mistakes and only earlier states fix bad data.
